articles.title: Peter Otobong: From Coder to Fintech Systems Engineer | TechCabal
articles.text:
The technology was not the problem.
For Peter Otobong and his team at Fraqtion Finance, the idea was simple enough: allow people to pool money to finance real-world trade, such as a Chinese company buying lithium from Nigeria. The software could be built. The architecture could be designed. The engineers could make the system work.
But then came the questions that code could not answer.
Who would license it? Who would regulate it? Where would the capital come from? Which financial institutions would support it? And how would the technology fit into the systems that already governed the movement of money and commodities across borders?
The project never launched.
For Otobong, however, its failure became one of the most important lessons of his career.
“The biggest constraints are not necessarily technical. The biggest constraints are normally the systems in which the technology is going to operate in,” he says.
It was a lesson that would change the way he looked at his profession. Technology, he began to understand, does not exist in isolation. A piece of software may work perfectly and still fail if the business around it is wrong, if regulation does not permit it, if institutions cannot support it or if the people it was built for cannot use it.
For someone who had once dreamed of becoming a mad scientist, it was an important realisation.
As a boy, Otobong had imagined science as an almost limitless frontier. He wanted to build things, explore strange possibilities and push beyond what was already known.
“A scientist who is doing a lot of stuff, like going to space, trying to imitate aliens,” he says, recalling the kind of scientist he wanted to become.
The inspiration came largely from the cartoons and animations he watched growing up. They gave him a world in which imagination was not constrained by what was immediately possible.
Years later, that instinct to build remains. But the problems Otobong is interested in have become more complicated.
He is no longer simply asking whether something can be built.
He wants to know whether it can survive the world around it.
And that distinction has taken him from tinkering with computers as a child to writing software, building blockchain systems, developing communities of African technologists and working on financial infrastructure for businesses moving money across borders.
Finding a path into tech
The computer laboratory at his primary school was supposed to teach Otobong how to use a computer. Instead, it left him wondering how the machine itself worked.
In Primary Four, his school began taking students to the laboratory to learn basic applications such as Microsoft Word and Excel. While other pupils were learning how to use the programmes, Otobong found himself more interested in what was happening beneath the screen.
“That was where my interests in computers really grew,” he says. “It was my first physical interaction with this imagination I’ve always had to become sort of a mad scientist.”
The laptop that would finally give that curiosity somewhere to go came years later.
In 2014, an uncle gave him one, and for the first time, Otobong had a computer he could explore on his own. He began teaching himself how to code, moving from curiosity about computers to actually building things with them.
“2014 was when I actually started getting my hands dirty with C++ and writing code and also getting introduced to how to design web applications,” he says.
Yet even then, software engineering did not feel like a career to him.
He had grown up in an environment where the profession was barely visible. The people around him followed careers he could easily name: government work, accounting, engineering and jobs in the oil industry. Software was something he enjoyed experimenting with, but he had never seen anyone close to him turn that interest into a profession.
“I grew up in an environment where it was very strange to say somebody’s a software engineer,” he says. “I don’t have any relative or friend who was into IT.”
So, when the time came to choose a university course in 2015, Otobong did what many young Nigerians do when the path ahead is still unclear: he followed a familiar route that still left room for his curiosity.
A family friend introduced him to electrical and electronics engineering at the University of Port Harcourt, Rivers State in Southern Nigeria. The course offered a bridge between the physical systems that fascinated him and the computers he had begun teaching himself to understand.
For the next five years, he studied the discipline. But it was outside the classroom, during an internship, that Otobong would begin to understand where he truly belonged.
From hardware to software
In 2019, Otobong interned at Atopets Automation, a robotics and automation company in Port Harcourt. He worked with microcontrollers, Arduino boards, ESPs and Raspberry Pi, building systems that could respond to the physical world.
But he found himself increasingly drawn to the software behind the hardware.
“I discovered that I love the hardware, but I also love the process of writing software to make the hardware work,” he says.
That realisation pushed him deeper into software and shaped his final-year project: a facial-recognition system that could identify authorised users and control access to a smart door.
Then, in 2020, he was selected as a Google Student Developer Lead at the University of Port Harcourt. The programme exposed him to developers across Africa and, for the first time, showed him that software engineering could be a viable career.
“I got to see people who were in the software field as a full-time career, and they were doing well,” he says. “And so it just changed something in my mind because I can now see that I can actually build a career out of this.”
From building systems to building communities
After graduating in 2021, Otobong’s first professional break came at the African Blockchain Centre for Developers (ABCD). A friend had told him about a blockchain training programme, and he applied, initially expecting to learn alongside other young developers.
He was selected as one of the first 14 people in the cohort. But ABCD soon realised that Otobong was bringing more to the programme than a willingness to learn. He already had experience with technology and, importantly, with bringing people together around it.
“They reached out and asked if I wanted to join the team, not just to learn about blockchain, but to work on the technical side and with other developers.”
The invitation marked a subtle shift in his career. Otobong entered ABCD as a learner but soon found himself on the other side of the learning process, working as a technical and developer advocate.
At first, his work centred on understanding blockchain technologies such as Ethereum and helping others make sense of a field that was still unfamiliar to many developers in Nigeria. But as ABCD’s work evolved from training and advocacy to building software and tools for clients in the blockchain space, so did Otobong’s responsibilities.
He began working with organisations to define what they needed, translate those needs into technical requirements and scope projects. He also helped vet developers, write code and coordinate technical teams.
The progression was gradual, but significant. He was no longer simply learning how technology worked; he was learning how to make it work for other people.
Eventually, Otobong grew into a technical lead role, taking greater responsibility for technical delivery while helping organisations find, evaluate and manage the developers who would build their products.
It was around this time that another idea began taking shape in his mind: technology was not only about the things you built. It was also about the people and communities that made building possible.
Building a community
While at ABCD, Otobong became interested in Blacks In Technology, a global non-profit that supports Black people pursuing careers in technology. A friend regularly posted about the organisation, prompting him to reach out to Dennis Schultz, an executive director.
Otobong told Schultz about his experience leading the Google community at the University of Port Harcourt, his work at ABCD and an impact project he wanted to pursue.
The conversation led to a call with Schultz, which opened the door for him to establish a Blacks In Technology chapter in Nigeria.
One of his first priorities was helping developers who wanted to get started but lacked the equipment to do so. The idea was personal. His own journey in tech had started with the HP Mini laptop his uncle gave him in 2014, so he wanted to give other developers a similar opportunity.
“They approved $10,000 to support us in buying some used laptops,” he says. “But each time they tried to send the money to Nigeria, it was flagged for risk and then reversed. It happened on three occasions.”
The failed transfers meant the laptop project could not go ahead, so Otobong and the chapter turned to events, programmes and online learning opportunities instead.
“We had to focus on doing events and programmes, sometimes virtually. We would get vouchers because back then BIT had a lot of partnerships with the likes of Coursera and other different platforms.”
Otobong says the approach helped the community grow. Within a short period, he says the Nigerian chapter had close to 500 members and was recognised as the fastest-growing international chapter in 2022.
The experience also changed how Otobong thought about creating impact in technology. He began to see that building the people around technology was as important as building the technology itself.
“The most important way to build impact or create value is to build community and ecosystems.”
For Otobong, communities create the talent and opportunities that allow an ecosystem to grow.
“We can’t build in silos. Community is the best tool for shaping the ecosystem. And when you shape the ecosystem, what you do is that you also shape and build the talent.”
Building for a different reality
In 2023, Otobong left ABCD and spent several months thinking about what he wanted to do next. He was unsure whether to continue pursuing software engineering or move towards something more focused on business and strategy.
“I was thinking, should I still try to look for new opportunities and jobs to just go deep into tech, or should I pivot into something that has more business- and strategy-related, or just try to become a founder of something else?” he said.
He eventually chose to stay in technology. In January 2024, he joined LTO Network, a Dutch blockchain company focused on real-world assets, as a senior software engineer.
At LTO, he worked on systems that allowed assets such as land and legal documents to be represented on the blockchain. One of the projects was GoLand Registry, which was designed to allow property owners to create verifiable records of their assets and use them to access financing.
Otobong’s role was to help adapt the platform for Burkina Faso. That meant thinking beyond the technology itself: how people would use it, how it would work with limited internet access and how it could fit into existing government processes.
“I had a lot of autonomy at LTO where I could think through problems, I could create an architecture, I could present it to the team, and they would decide what the best approach was.”
The work exposed him to a different kind of engineering problem. The challenge was no longer simply whether something could be built, but whether it could work in the environment for which it was intended.
GoLand had been developed in collaboration with the United Nations for Afghanistan before being adapted for Burkina Faso. Otobong says its adoption depended not only on the technology, but also on government support and existing administrative systems.
LTO was also where Otobong built the project he is most proud of in his career: a relay protocol that allowed wallets to communicate with one another and exchange files and other assets, rather than just cryptocurrency.
“I would say it was something I was proud of because people were using it. So, when I see people look at their wallet balances and some people have a lot of their money inside the wallet, and they are really looking forward to the progress, when is this going to go live? Just knowing that you are building something that has value and you know has like a long-term use case for a lot of people made me really proud.”
After his time at LTO, Otobong joined Esca Finance, a fintech focused on cross-border payments, foreign exchange and liquidity for businesses in emerging markets, in 2026 in a full-time role. He now works on cross-border finance and liquidity, as the company builds financial rails to help businesses manage currency conversions and reduce their exposure to foreign exchange volatility.
His work there draws on the experiences that have shaped his career so far. Beyond building the technology, he has had to understand the financial system in which it operates, including compliance, fraud mitigation and the processes involved in verifying customers and businesses.
“I have learned that being a software engineer is not just about being technical, I have to also understand the domain in which I am operating.”
From software engineer to systems thinker
Looking back across his career, Otobong can identify things he would have done differently. Chief among them is that he wishes he had challenged himself earlier — and dreamed bigger.
“I really wished that I had challenged myself more. Let’s say it’s one of my regrets.”
For a while, he says, he kept too many options open instead of committing fully to a particular direction. He watched some of his friends go deep into fields such as artificial intelligence while he remained interested in the connections between different technologies.
It is not that he believes he chose the wrong path. If anything, he has become more convinced that his path was right. What he regrets is not pursuing it with enough conviction.
“It’s not because the path I chose was wrong; my path is still very correct, but I feel like I should have had more conviction.”
That conviction has also changed what he believes it means to be a software engineer.
When he began writing code as a teenager, the computer was the thing he wanted to understand. Over the years, the questions have become larger. He now thinks about the businesses, institutions, regulations and people that software must work with before it can create any meaningful impact.
It is a shift from seeing technology as a tool to seeing it as part of a larger system — one that can succeed only when the pieces around it work, too.
At ESCA Finance, that is the perspective he brings to his work in cross-border finance and liquidity. It is also the clearest expression yet of the engineer he has become: not someone concerned only with whether the code works, but with whether the system it powers can work.
“As much as I call myself a software engineer, I would say I see myself as a systems engineer. Because I am no longer just thinking about software as code, but I’m thinking about software as systems.”
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks. articles.title: "Le dernier argument face à Google Maps s'effondre" : Apple impose ses publicités dans Plans, et la colère monte
articles.text:
"Le dernier argument face à Google Maps s'effondre" : Apple impose ses publicités dans Plans, et la colère monte
Ça y est, c'est fait. Apple a glissé des publicités dans Plans, son application de cartographie. Le déploiement a démarré aux États-Unis et au Canada, aucune option de désactivation n'existe, et les abonnés payants encaissent mal la nouvelle.
Le projet, que nous évoquions déjà en février 2025, a pris forme. Apple a confirmé au site 9to5Mac que les premières publicités apparaissent dans Plans depuis le 25 août, avec une montée en charge progressive dans les semaines à venir. Plus d'un milliard de recherches commerciales transitent chaque mois par l'application, selon Apple. Une requête sur deux débouche sur une action concrète.
Enchères au mot-clé, badge bleu et zéro opt-out
Les annonces se glissent à deux endroits : dans les "Lieux suggérés" dès l'ouverture du champ de recherche, et en tête des résultats après une requête. Un badge bleu "Ad" les signale, à raison d'une seule publicité par recherche. Le système repose sur des enchères par mot-clé, sans budget minimum.
Pour attirer les premiers commerces, Apple accorde 15 % de crédit mensuel (plafonné à 1 000 dollars) pendant un an aux inscrits avant le 11 octobre 2026. Certaines catégories restent bannies : services à domicile, jeux d'argent, alcool, cryptomonnaies, religion.
Sur Reddit, la pilule passe mal. Un abonné Apple One à 50 dollars par mois résume l'amertume générale : "Ce que j'adore, c'est de payer 50 dollars par mois et de voir quand même des pubs dans Plans et News."
	
Ce que j'adore, c'est de payer 50 dollars par mois d'Apple One et de voir quand même des pubs dans Plans et News.
Plusieurs internautes soulignent que l'absence de publicité était le dernier argument tangible de Plans face à Google Maps et Waze, deux applications déjà truffées d'annonces mais autrement plus complètes. "Google Maps est largement plus précis et fonctionnel. Le seul avantage de Plans, c'était l'absence de pub", tranche un autre.
La perspective d'un futur palier "sans pub" facturé plus cher, sur le modèle de YouTube Premium ou des offres TV, revient dans les commentaires comme une quasi-certitude. Un constat plus structurel circule aussi : Apple anticiperait une érosion de ses commissions sur les achats intégrés, fragilisées par les régulations européennes et américaines, et chercherait à compenser via la publicité.
La France épargnée, pour l'instant
Le déploiement reste cantonné à l'Amérique du Nord, sans calendrier pour l'Europe. En février 2026, la Commission européenne a estimé que Plans et Apple Ads ne constituaient pas des passerelles suffisamment importantes au sens du Digital Markets Act, faute d'audience sur le continent. Apple dispose donc d'une latitude réglementaire confortable pour étendre le dispositif, d'autant que la plateforme Ads on Maps s'appuie sur Apple Business, actif dans plus de 200 pays depuis avril 2026. L'infrastructure est prête, seul le calendrier manque.

articles.title: This 98-qubit quantum computer moves ions around to compute more efficiently
articles.text:
First look: Quantinuum's new Helios processor is a major engineering step for trapped-ion quantum computing, built to solve a problem that gets harder as systems grow: moving qubits through a machine without undermining their performance. The 98-qubit processor uses a four-way junction to route ions between memory and processing areas. It also relies on a control system that plans those movements while coordinating quantum operations. Together, the hardware and software give Helios more room to run operations in parallel than earlier trapped-ion designs.
Helios is the largest trapped-ion quantum computer demonstrated so far. Quantinuum, which is based in Cambridge, UK, and Broomfield, Colorado, previously demonstrated machines with 32 qubits in 2023 and 56 qubits in 2025.
The processor uses charged atoms, known as ions, as qubits. Electromagnetic fields hold the ions above the chip, and laser pulses carry out the quantum gates. Helios follows a quantum charge-coupled device, or QCCD, design. Instead of keeping every qubit in one fixed place, it stores ions in one part of the machine and moves them into separate areas for processing.
Its layout includes a ring-shaped memory region connected to two processing paths. The four-way X junction sits where those regions meet. Earlier QCCD designs could move ions through a line or loop. The new junction gives the system more possible routes and lets it handle multiple tasks at once.
That physical design is only part of the advance. Helios also uses software called Helios runtime to organize the work. The software determines when ions should move, where they should go and when laser operations should be performed. It must avoid routing conflicts while keeping the quantum circuit moving efficiently.
The design differs from superconducting quantum computers, where qubits are generally fixed in place and controlled by electrical signals. In a trapped-ion QCCD system, moving qubits is part of the calculation. The system must transport ions to the proper processing region before certain gates can be performed.
The approach is intended to reduce crosstalk, in which an operation on one qubit interferes with another. It also allows qubits to be measured and reset during a computation, which can help detect and correct errors before they spread. Because ions can be moved through the device, the system can also bring distant qubits together for operations.
Helios demonstrated calculations that known classical methods could not reproduce within practical time and power limits. The work involved random benchmark tests, not scientific or commercial applications. That distinction matters. The processor does not yet show that quantum computing can solve a useful business or research problem better than a classical computer.
The system is also far from fault-tolerant quantum computing. Practical systems are generally expected to require roughly a million qubits. The UK National Quantum Strategy has set a target for a fault-tolerant computer able to perform one trillion operations. Helios' longest reported computation involved about 4,000 operations on 98 qubits.
Scaling the technology would require linking many QCCD devices through quantum connections. Proposed designs envision two-dimensional grids with more qubits and junctions, but that would bring fresh problems. Ions could face traffic bottlenecks as they move through the system, while voltage controls would need to remain extremely precise across a much larger machine.
Helios is not a practical fault-tolerant quantum computer. It is, however, a meaningful breakthrough in the hardware and control systems needed to scale trapped-ion processors.

articles.title: AliExpress allegedly uses your browser's audio system to fingerprint your PC — hidden code runs even when no sound is playing
articles.text:
AliExpress allegedly uses your browser's audio system to fingerprint your PC — hidden code runs even when no sound is playing
Hidden code allegedly gathers detailed device data.
Chinese multinational tech giant Alibaba has been accused of tracking web users after a developer discovered its global online marketplace running hidden audio processes that could be used for sophisticated audio fingerprinting. While investigating an issue with his wireless headphones, Matt Callaghan found that opening an AliExpress webpage in Firefox or Chrome interfered with the multipoint Bluetooth audio feature.
As Callaghan explains in his blog post, “Normally the PC takes priority playing audio, with my phone being able to play audio when nothing is playing on the PC. Usually I listen to music on my phone but with notifications or YouTube playing through the PC.” However, shortly after loading the AliExpress homepage, audio from his phone would stop playing, despite no media playing on his PC. Closing the AliExpress tab immediately fixed the issue, while muting the tab, browser, or Windows did not seem to resolve it.
Their investigation began by inspecting various conventional media elements; however, he did not find any unusual activity. He also zeroed in on the fact that the problem would not begin immediately, but rather after the webpage had been sitting idle for a few seconds. He then moved on to inspect the Web Audio API to wrap the AudioContext constructor so that it would record whenever a page created an audio-processing context. They additionally wrapped AudioNode.prototype.connect() to see whether anything was connected to the context's audio destination.
Eventually, Callaghan found that the page was loading two suspicious scripts named collina.js and fireyejs.js, which appeared to be part of Alibaba's browser security and anti-abuse tooling. With some help from AI during his research, he found that the scripts built a Web Audio graph using a sawtooth oscillator to generate a waveform. An analyzer then measured the results after they passed through the browser's audio implementation, while another script read the resulting frequency data. The scripts also set the volume gain to zero, meaning there was no audible sound or noise, even though the browser continued actively processing the Web Audio graph.
Unlike autoplaying videos, there is no media element playing, which is why the browser's tab mute control does not help. However, the webpage continues performing live audio processing, keeping the Bluetooth audio path active and preventing multipoint Bluetooth headphones from switching between devices. Further investigation also uncovered code collecting information related to screen dimensions, device memory, browser plugins, WebGL rendering, supported audio and video formats, browser performance, mouse events, and more. The scripts also appear to serialize and encrypt the collected data before sending it to Alibaba's telemetry services using fetch() or sendBeacon() functions.
Following the discovery, Firefox said on X that its browser includes built-in protections against fingerprinting. The company pointed to a blog post explaining that Firefox 118, released in September 2023, introduced additional protections against Web Audio-based fingerprinting. Brave also claims to block audio fingerprinting by default. According to the browser maker, it does this by injecting randomized data into the browser's audio output, making the fingerprint appear different to websites and resetting the data between sessions.

Kunal Khullar is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. He is a long time technology journalist and reviewer specializing in PC components and peripherals, and welcomes any and every question around building a PC.

articles.title: Les routeurs Wi-Fi de Comcast peuvent désormais détecter les mouvements dans un logement
articles.text:
Un signal Wi-Fi ne va pas du routeur à l’ordinateur en ligne droite : il rebondit sur les murs, les meubles et les êtres vivants à portée. Traversez la pièce, et le signal qui revient au routeur n’est plus tout à fait le même. Il suffit alors d’un logiciel capable de comparer en continu ce signal pour savoir si quelque chose a bougé ou non autour de lui.
Comcast propose bel et bien cette fonctionnalité à ses abonnés américains, sous le nom de WiFi Motion. Son routeur maison, estampillé Xfinity, et jusqu’à trois appareils connectés fixes du réseau deviennent ainsi les points d’un maillage invisible, permettant de signaler les mouvements détectés entre eux.
L’IA générative crée du contenu en quelques secondes, mais souvent au prix de vos données personnelles. Avec Lumo AI, l’assistant européen de Proton, vos conversations restent 100 % confidentielles.
WiFi Motion n’est pas une nouveauté à proprement parler : Comcast propose cette détection de mouvement depuis 2025, et des abonnés en parlaient déjà fin 2024 sur Reddit. Ce qui change à la mi-août 2026, c’est son intégration dans Xfinity Shield, une nouvelle offre de sécurité maison qui la met bien plus en avant.
Ce que Comcast ne dit pas dans son communiqué
Pour expliquer le fonctionnement de sa nouveauté, l’opérateur américain donne l’image d’un ovale reliant votre box à l’un de vos appareils connectés, comme une enceinte ou un thermostat. Toute personne qui traverse cette zone perturbe le signal, ce qui déclenche une alerte. Aucune caméra, aucun micro, aucune image : le système ne prétend ni identifier l’individu qui bouge, ni situer précisément le mouvement, juste signaler qu’il se passe quelque chose.
Mais le communiqué de presse de Comcast reste assez vague sur certains détails, que Cybernews est allé chercher dans sa documentation : activer ce WiFi Motion revient à créer un registre horodaté des déplacements dans le logement. Plus gênant encore, la firme américaine précise qu’elle peut divulguer ces informations sur réquisition judiciaire, mandat de perquisition ou décision de justice, mais aussi dans le cadre d’un litige auquel elle serait partie prenante, ou d’une situation d’urgence.
L’opérateur affirme tout de même qu’il ne surveille pas « activement » les données que ses routeurs collectent. Il reconnaît en revanche en conserver une partie. Sa FAQ officielle précise qu’il garde l’historique des mouvements pendant sept jours, le temps que l’abonné puisse le consulter dans l’application Xfinity, mais ne détaille pas ce qu’il serait exactement en mesure de fournir à un enquêteur.
Le point le plus gênant tient sûrement dans cette formule glissée dans les conditions d’usage : aucune des situations de divulgation n’oblige Comcast à prévenir l’abonné. Les forces de l’ordre peuvent donc demander l’historique des mouvements à l’intérieur d’un domicile, l’obtenir, et le foyer concerné n’en saura rien.
Quoi qu’il en soit, Comcast ne fait rien d’illégal ici, et heureusement, la fonctionnalité est facultative. Mais voilà, quand on a une caméra chez soi, on l’achète en connaissance de cause, alors qu’ici les éléments de surveillance arrivent par une mise à jour gratuite dont tout le monde ne comprendra pas forcément les enjeux. Si un jour la fonctionnalité passe en activation par défaut, Comcast devra fournir des explications autrement plus claires à ses abonnés.

articles.title: The death of the human web? Report finds over a third of web pages pushed live since the launch of ChatGPT show evidence of being written by AI
articles.text:
The death of the human web? Report finds over a third of web pages pushed live since the launch of ChatGPT show evidence of being written by AI
AI is writing the web
- AI authorship is increasingly employed for web pages, Pew Research Center report claims
- Over 33% of pages published since the launch of ChatGPT reportedly show signs of AI generation
- Of the 10,000-page sample used in the study, 10% of pages had signs of AI authorship
An incredible 35% of web pages published since the launch of ChatGPT show signs of AI authorship, new research has claimed.
A study from the Pew Research Center, which used automated tools to assess a sample of 10,000 web pages, also found that in the entire sample – based on data from the Common Crawl project – almost 10% of all pages had signs of AI creation.
The “How Much of the Internet Is Written With AI?” report also found that certain types of websites are more likely to feature some AI generation, while detecting some of the key fingerprints of AI-generated text, which goes beyond em dashes.
AI is writing more and more web pages
The report – which was compiled using a machine learning model tasked with looking for signs of AI authorship – found that 9.6% of all pages in the sample of 10,000 appeared to have been written by AI. While that may seem a small amount, the sample from Common Crawl dates back to the beginning of the World Wide Web, over 30 years ago.
In keeping with other research (such as AI on the Internet), the data indicates that “large shares of recently published pages on the internet were likely written or substantially edited by AI.”
Reassuringly, the data highlights the interesting point that the majority of the suspected AI-generated web pages published in 2026 are .com domains and, as such typically commercial. In contrast, just 1% are .edu (US-based educational facilities) and 0.8% are .gov.
Is it written by AI?
Using its evaluation of 490,000 English-language web pages, the Pew Research Center also established some more useful indicators (“common features”) of AI text generation.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The em dash is regularly held up as an example of AI writing, as is the use of the Oxford comma. The em dash appears “twice as frequently” in pages published since 2023, while Oxford commas have a 63% increase. The report authors note that these aren’t solitary indicators (“Humans use these in their writing too!”)
Other “tells” offer a more reliable giveaway of AI-generated writing, as demonstrated by the report. Certain words and trends are listed by the research, including "delve," "interplay," and "testament," which have apparently “more than doubled in usage.” The report lists numerous examples of “AI-typical vocabulary.”
Meanwhile, the negative parallelism, which you might have seen as “it’s not just X, it’s Y,” has almost trebled in use.
It might be increasingly difficult to identify an AI-generated web page these days, but if it comes from a .edu or .gov domain, it is overall more likely to have been written by a human.

Christian Cawley has extensive experience as a writer and editor in consumer electronics, IT and entertainment media. He has contributed to TechRadar since 2017 and has been published in Computer Weekly, Linux Format, ComputerActive, and other publications.
He currently heads up the team at smart home website Matter Alpha, and writes about retro gaming at Gaming Retro.

articles.title: Apple's new desktop computers are designed specifically for local AI development
articles.text:
The Mac mini and Mac Studio occupy two distinct points in Apple’s lineup of desktops, but lately, they’ve had something in common: They’re popular for local AI inference and software development thanks to the advantages of their unified memory architecture and the fast CPUs and GPUs on their systems-on-a-chip.
Today, Apple announced new iterations of both desktops, along with two new chips: the M6, the first 2nm chip in Apple’s M-series lineup for Macs, and the M5 Ultra, now the most powerful chip in the lineup for most things—especially AI workloads.
There aren’t any major new features for either machine. This is just a specs bump. But based on how Apple is presenting these refreshes, they’re leaning hard into those use cases, which weren’t even a thought when earlier iterations were first engineered.
The devices’ popularity for production inference took off after macOS 26.2 shipped last December. According to Apple’s release notes, 26.2 enabled “low-latency communication between Thunderbolt 5 hosts for use cases including distributed AI inference using MLX.” Thunderbolt 5 is a very fast wired data connection, and MLX is an open source array framework designed to help machine learning workflows take full advantage of the M-series chips’ unified memory.
Since then, both hobbyists and professional developers and researchers have been essentially daisy-chaining Mac minis or Mac Studios to run inference on local large language models that are much bigger than anything that could run a single mass-market device—providing an alternative to ultra-beefy specialized hardware featuring specialized Nvidia GPUs.

articles.title: Arduino Announces Pre-Orders for VENTUNO Q Edge AI Platform
articles.text:
Tuesday, August 25th 2026
	
		
	
	
	
Arduino Announces Pre-Orders for VENTUNO Q Edge AI Platform
Arduino S.r.l., a subsidiary of Qualcomm Technologies, Inc., today opened pre-orders for Arduino VENTUNO Q, its most advanced edge AI platform to date, powered by the Qualcomm Dragonwing IQ8 Series. Now available worldwide, VENTUNO Q was built for developers, prioritizing familiarity and ease of use with the right software, accessories and extensions. 
One Board to Sense, Decide, and Act
The VENTUNO Q has a dual-brain architecture, pairing a Dragonwing IQ-8275 processor, delivering up to 40 dense TOPS of AI performance, with 16 GB LPDDR5 memory, 64 GB eMMC and expandable M.2 NVMe storage, alongside a dedicated STM32H5 real-time microcontroller, enabling systems that don't just interpret sensor data but respond to it physically, immediately and offline.The board ships with preloaded Ubuntu, distributed by Canonical. The Arduino App Lab offers a fast path to a working prototype. Developers can also elect to utilize VS Code, native Linux tools, or any existing workflow as well. On the MCU side, the Arduino Core on Zephyr RTOS is designed to provide deterministic, real-time control of motors, CAN-FD, PWM and high-speed GPIO.
"For twenty-one years, Arduino has taken complex technology and made it simple enough to build something real. VENTUNO Q is that same mission, applied to the most consequential technology of our time. With VENTUNO Q, we are giving developers, educators and innovators the tools to build machines that don't just think, but do," said Fabio Violante, VP & GM, Arduino, Qualcomm Technologies, Inc.
Agentic AI for the Physical World
Through Arduino App Lab, developers can run a curated library of NPU-optimized models out of the box, spanning LLMs, VLMs, speech recognition, and object and gesture detection; bring their own GGUF-format model from Hugging Face; or train and quantize custom models via the integrated Edge Impulse Studio. LLMs and VLMs can also be deployed in just a few lines of code using the Qualcomm Gen AI Developer Tool (GenieX), Qualcomm Technologies' open-source on-device Gen AI runtime. The platform has been designed and validated for commercial deployment across robotics, industrial edge AI, smart cities, AI vision systems, and education - powering applications from autonomous mobile robots and predictive maintenance to real-time quality inspection and hands-on STEM learning.
'Works with Arduino': The Dragonwing IQ8 SOM Pathway from Prototype to Production
Once a VENTUNO Q design is ready for commercial deployment, the same Dragonwing IQ8 processor will soon be available in production-grade SOM form factors from partners, preserving the software stack, AI models, and application logic built during prototyping. SECO, a leading provider of edge computing and AI industrial solutions, and Toradex, a specialist in industrial-grade SOMs, are among the first to support this pathway under the "Works with Arduino" program.
"The Dragonwing IQ8 Series is designed to support early development through commercial deployment," said Nakul Duggal, EVP and Group GM, Automotive, Industrial and Embedded IoT, Qualcomm Technologies, Inc. "The 'Works with Arduino' program gives developers and partners a practical way to bring innovations built on Dragonwing IQ8 into commercial products, helping accelerate development and commercialization across our ecosystem."
"At SECO, we've spent decades helping companies turn great ideas into products that ship and perform in the real world - and doing so alongside partners who share that mission is what excites us most. Joining the 'Works with Arduino' program on the Dragonwing IQ8 platform brings together Arduino's openness and ease of use with SECO's production-grade engineering, helping enable developers to prototype quickly and scale with confidence. We're proud to be among the first to make this journey from idea to volume production truly seamless," said Massimo Mauri, CEO of SECO.
"With VENTUNO Q, Arduino is making high-performance AI and robotics accessible to a broad community of developers. Toradex is excited to extend that journey to production of mission-critical applications: Aquila pairs the new Dragonwing IQ8 Series with our high-performance Aquila architecture, giving embedded developers a path from prototype to reliable, long-lived industrial and edge AI products," said Samuel Imgrueth, CEO of Toradex.
Beyond prototyping, VENTUNO Q has been designed for commercial deployment across robotics, industrial edge AI, smart cities and connected homes, AI vision systems, and education, powering everything from autonomous mobile robots and predictive maintenance to real-time quality inspection and hands-on STEM learning.
Availability and Pricing
VENTUNO Q is available to pre-order now from the Arduino Store and official distribution partners including DigiKey, Farnell, Robu.in, Mouser, and RS.

articles.title: Bundesbank will digitalen Euro und Wero kombinieren – doch ein Problem bleibt
articles.text:
Digitaler Euro soll in Wero-Wallet: Bundesbank plant Kombi gegen Paypal und Co.
Für mehr europäische Unabhängigkeit beim digitalen Bezahlen sollten aus Sicht der Bundesbank die europäische Paypal-Alternative Wero und der digitale Euro miteinander verzahnt werden. „Denkbar wäre beispielsweise, den digitalen Euro in die Wero Wallet zu integrieren“, sagte Bundesbank-Vorstand Lutz Lienenkämper in Frankfurt bei einem Symposium der Deutschen Bundesbank zum Zahlungsverkehr. „Das könnte die Reichweite europäischer Zahlungsangebote erhöhen und dazu beitragen, dass neue Lösungen nicht nebeneinanderstehen, sondern nahtlos zusammenwirken.“
Wero wird von der European Payments Initiative (EPI), einem Zusammenschluss von Banken und Zahlungsdienstleistern, vorangetrieben. Seit Anfang Juli 2024 bietet Wero nach dem Muster des US-Konkurrenten Paypal vor allem direkte mobile Geldzahlungen von Mensch zu Mensch an. Inzwischen kann Wero auch bei etlichen Händlern zum Einkaufen im Netz genutzt werden, ähnlich wie Kreditkarten, Apple Pay, Google Pay oder andere vergleichbare Dienste.
Wero-Nutzerzahlen sind noch gering
Nach jüngsten Angaben gibt es bislang 57 Millionen registrierte Wero-Nutzer in Belgien, Frankreich und Deutschland. An der Einführung in den Niederlanden, Luxemburg und Österreich wird gearbeitet. Noch habe Wero auch hierzulande das Potenzial nicht ausgeschöpft, stellte Lienenkämper fest. „Der Markthochlauf bleibt daher eine Aufgabe, die mit Nachdruck verfolgt werden muss.“
Der digitale Euro stößt auf Kritik
Dass die Europäische Zentralbank (EZB) parallel seit Jahren an einem digitalen Euro als Alternative zum Bargeld arbeitet, finden Kritiker auch angesichts der Kosten fragwürdig. Mit einem digitalen Euro wollen die Euro-Notenbanken privaten Anbietern vor allem aus den USA wie Paypal, Mastercard und Visa, die derzeit den Markt für digitale Zahlungen in Europa dominieren, ein europäisches Angebot entgegensetzen. Angepeilt ist die Einführung des digitalen Euro für 2029.
Der digitale Euro sei wichtig, sagte Lienenkämper: „Ein digitaler Euro ist Zentralbankgeld für den digitalen Raum: allgemein zugänglich, sicher, europäisch und mit hohem Datenschutz – als Ergänzung zu privaten Zahlungslösungen und auch zum Bargeld, nicht aber als deren Ersatz.“

articles.title: Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20 now available for pre-order in Canada
articles.text:
Asus announced when its latest gaming handheld, the ROG Xbox Ally X20, will be available ahead of Gamescom on Aug. 25. Moreover, we finally learned the price — an eye-watering $1,899 in Canada.
And if for some reason you wanted to spend even more money, Asus also has a bundle with the Ally X20 and the ROG Xreal R1 Edition 20 augmented reality (AR) glasses.
The Xbox Ally X20 sports a translucent black chassis with gold-accented internals and debuts ROG’s Nebula HDR OLED display. The screen measures in at 7.4 inches with a 1080p resolution and up to a 120Hz refresh rate.
Other specs include an AMD Ryzen AI Z2 Extreme processor, 24GB of RAM, 1TB of storage, and an 80Wh battery. Those are very similar specs to the ROG Xbox Ally X, with the big difference being the larger OLED display.
Meanwhile, the ROG Xreal R1 Edition 20 glasses sport 0.55-inch Sony Micro OLED displays with a per-eye resolution of 1920×1080 pixels and a 120Hz refresh rate, or 240Hz with frame boost. The glasses also feature Bose speakers and a mic with noise cancellation.
As mentioned up top, the ROG Xbox Ally X20 on its own costs $1,899 in Canada, while the bundle with the AR glasses jumps up to $3,499. Notably, that makes it quite a bit more expensive than the Xbox Ally X at $1,499, and even more than the regular Xbox Ally at $799.
While MobileSyrup liked both the Xbox Ally models when they launched last year, we also cited the high price as an issue. The Xbox Ally X20 costs even more without adding a ton to the formula, so I’m not sure it’s worth the money.
ROG Xbox Ally Canadian review: Great handheld that costs too much
Still, if you want to buy one, the standalone Xbox Ally X20 will be available for pre-order starting today at Best Buy, and on Sept. 24 at the Asus Store, while the bundle with the ROG Xreal R1 Edition 20 AR glasses will be available for pre-order starting Sept. 24. Both begin shipping on October 15.

articles.title: India's Ringg gets backing from Peak XV as it pushes voice AI past the phone call | TechCrunch
articles.text:
More than 76% of consumers in India prefer talking to businesses over a phone call, according to a recent study from Truecaller. Since voice is still consumers’ preferred way to communicate, that leaves a big opportunity to automate support and outreach calls using voice AI in the country. Voice AI startup Ringg, which already processes 20 million call attempts a month, is betting that volume keeps climbing over the coming months, and it just raised more money on that belief.
The company said today it has landed $10 million from Peak XV Partners as an extension of its Series A. It had previously raised $5.5 million in a Series A round earlier this year, bringing the round’s total to $15.5 million.
Ringg started life as a text-to-speech startup called DesiVocal, but training its own speech models proved expensive, so the founders moved up the stack — building voice AI agents for enterprises instead. Indian fintech Cred became its first customer, and Ringg has since signed Indian startups like Flipkart, Practo, Groww, and Policybazaar.
“At the start, we were doing high-volume, low-complexity use cases like outbound calling, lead qualification, loan collection, and more. We quickly realized these are not sticky use cases, and so it’s always going to be a price game,” the startup’s co-founder Siddharth Tripathi told TechCrunch.
Ringg still serves some of those simpler use cases, but it has set its sights on more complex workflows: appointment booking for healthcare clinics, abandoned-cart recovery for e-commerce sites, and onboarding/KYC (“know your customer”) checks for fintech apps.
Tripathi said Ringg’s voice agent now runs across 1,200 clinics for the healthcare app Practo, helping patients book visits or follow up on next steps post-visit.
Voice calls still make up over 70% of Ringg’s business, but the startup has started branching into other channels, including chat and WhatsApp. For some clients like Shell, it’s also automating browser-based support requests.
“We are trying to position ourselves as a platform for agents that bring outcomes or get things done rather than voice agents for enterprises,” Tripathi said.
Most of Ringg’s customers are based in India, with a handful in the Middle East and the U.S. But the startup isn’t trying to sell directly to U.S. companies; instead, it wants to partner with global capability centers in India — the offshore hubs multinationals increasingly lean on for back-office and support work — to sell automation capacity alongside human support.
Tripathi said the company builds its own speech recognition and generation models and would eventually like to own the full voice stack, including infrastructure and deployment. For now, though, that remains too costly, so the product works as an orchestration layer, routing tasks to different models depending on the use case.
Rishen Kapoor, a principal at Peak XV, said that because Ringg started as a research lab building its own models, that technical depth shows up in the complex use cases it’s now tackling.
“Because of the technical capabilities, they can actually do these hard-won enterprise workflows end to end. They can complete these higher-value tasks like merchant onboarding, like L1 and L2 support, with quality and with consistency,” Kapoor told TechCrunch.
Voice AI in India is a crowded field. Model makers, including Deepgram, ElevenLabs, Cartesia, and local players like Sarvam and Smallest.ai, are all jockeying for pole position. Orchestration-focused startups like Bolna and Blue Machines are chasing the same layer Ringg occupies, while sector-focused players like Gnani and Arrowhead concentrate heavily on finance.
That layered stack — model makers, orchestrators, and application-layer players all trying to lock in enterprise workflows — is itself the story. The money and the defensibility increasingly sit with whoever owns the customer relationship and the outcome.
Ringg currently has 40 employees, with more than 15 hired in the last three months. The startup is hiring for forward-deployed engineer roles that combine technical chops with product management skills, along with researchers focused on bringing down the cost of running its models.

articles.title: SA AI startup Verascient raises $1.2m pre-seed funding to help companies build better teams - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
South African startup Verascient has raised ZAR19.5 million (US$1.2 million) in pre-seed funding to help companies build faster and more capable teams using AI.
Founded by Keagan Stokoe and Emile Ferreira, the Cape Town-based Verascient delivers the operating system and expertise companies need to successfully leverage the best of AI.
The startup turns knowledge scattered across documents, systems and individuals into shared organisational context, then builds the workflows and agents that allow teams to use it in their day-to-day work.
Verascient’s oversubscribed ZAR19.5 million round was backed by Founder Collective, Andrena Ventures, Cambridge Enterprise and Summit Ventures, with participation from Alan Knott-Craig, Shayne Mann and other select angel investors.
“At the centre of Verascient’s technology is a temporal knowledge graph designed to build and maintain a comprehensive understanding of an organisation, ensuring that information that was once scattered quickly becomes securely available to AI agents while preserving the history, permissions and provenance behind the information,” said Ferreira.
“There is a significant difference between giving employees access to an AI tool, and building a company that can operate intelligently with AI. Verascient bridges that gap by working directly with businesses to understand how their people and processes operate, and providing the secure infrastructure that enables AI agents to understand the organisation, work within its existing systems and access controls, and deliver valuable results.”
Stokoe said the raise would enable the startup to build a “small, exceptional team of engineers and AI builders”.
“We are looking for high-agency people with the curiosity, technical depth and ambition to build something meaningful to solve real-world problems. We’re looking for the top one per cent of AI talent, who are excited to take genuine ownership with the freedom to do the best work of their lives,” he said.

articles.title: Ten years of UPI: The infrastructure that quietly rewrote how India lives
articles.text:
Ten years of UPI: The infrastructure that quietly rewrote how India lives
Ten years after its launch, UPI has become far more than a payment system. It has transformed everyday transactions, enabled commerce during the pandemic and taken India’s digital public infrastructure to the world.
In 2018, I moved back to Google to work on GPay. At the time, I could never have imagined that an instant real-time payment system developed in India by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) under the aegis of RBI with many notable individual contributions, would become so big and transform so much.
I remember trying to explain to colleagues abroad why a real-time, interoperable system built on a public utility model would work at a scale nothing else in the world had attempted. But ten years later, the undeniable proof is there for everyone to see.
UPI went far beyond a faster way to pay. It became the infrastructure underneath how more than a billion people's lives transformed, almost instantaneously.
The numbers alone tell part of that story: annual UPI transaction volume has gone from 1.78 crore in FY17 to over 24,162 crore in FY26, a nearly 13,000-fold increase, with transaction value rising from Rs 7,000 crore to around Rs 314 lakh crore in the same period, according to Ministry of Finance. In July 2026 alone, UPI recorded 2,366 crore transactions, the highest monthly volume in its decade-long journey.
Perhaps the clearest way to understand UPI’s social and economic impact is to remember the pandemic. India’s ability to navigate that period keeping households supported, small businesses functioning and everyday commerce moving, would have been materially harder without it.
As one of the world’s largest and most densely connected societies went into lockdown, the challenge was not only to contain a public health emergency but also to ensure that money could continue to move when people could not. At a time when people were sanitising groceries, parcels, door handles, and currency notes, handling cash had become another source of anxiety. This mattered especially for migrant workers who went back to their towns without any means to earn a living but many employers could support them through the ease of UPI payments. UPI made sure you didn't have to go anywhere. Groceries, medicines, a doctor's teleconsultation, rent, and even care packages, all of them got settled instantly.
What now feels ordinary was, at that moment, extraordinarily important. It made money fluid when people had to stay apart and helped preserve a measure of economic and social continuity in a year defined by uncertainty.
That same payment system has reshaped daily life well after the pandemic. Street vendors don't need cash and migrant workers send money home instantly. No more standing in queues and worrying about losing that hard earned daily wage. Now, the transformation has become invisible. We pay bills, split bills, pay school fees and even tip a delivery rider by just whipping out our phones and not thinking twice about what went behind it. It's not just the ease of use, but also the safety and dignity of those small daily decisions that used to carry real cost in more ways than one.
UPI now processes over 20 billion transactions a month, across 504 million users and 65 million merchants, accounting for 84% of India's digital retail payments and nearly half of all real-time payment volume globally, according to BCG/NPCI Global Benchmark Report.
No other country has built anything close to this at this speed. That scale has also meant deeper institutional reach: the number of banks live on UPI has grown from 44 in FY17 to 703 today, according to Ministry of Finance.
Not just spending, but that same shift has also happened when it comes to how India invests. The retail SIP transactions in India through UPI grew by almost 177% last year alone. Free and fast flow of money through UPI has been helpful for the growth of both mutual funds and broking transactions as everyone has easy access from their mobile phones. That's financial inclusion actually happening, not as policy language, but as habit.
And this gargantuan success is now transforming other countries. For the past many decades now, India was perceived as the biggest exporter of finished digital products, engineers and IT services. UPI has taken that story and levelled it up. India is now exporting the underlying infrastructure itself. UPI is already live in eight-plus countries, including the UAE, Singapore, France and the UK, according to Ministry of Finance.
We have signed digital public infrastructure cooperation agreements with 23 nations, with cross-border UPI volumes growing 20x in a single year, according to NPCI International/PIB data on UPI's global footprint and cross-border transaction growth, FY23–FY25.
When the CEO of PayPal, one of the pioneers of online transactions, said "everywhere I go, India comes up," he wasn't far from the truth. UPI is the first, and possibly the biggest, payment system integrated into the PayPal World. Countries aren't just admiring what India built, but going a step further and partnering with us to build it for them.
It's about more than just payments. This is a real, working demonstration that India can conceive, build, and scale deep technology infrastructure, not just service it for others, at a level the rest of the world now studies and adopts. It's a much-needed reminder that capability does not need to stay contained to a single sector. We are capable of applying the engineering discipline, design thinking, and scale-first approach that built UPI to achieving India’s ambitions for the future. These can be in AI or anything else.
The next decade will see UPI go beyond being just a payment rail. The most immediate shift is likely to be international. Imagine a global UPI that makes remittances and merchant payments across countries as instant and inexpensive as domestic ones.
However, the strongest foundation for the next phase can be built on the domestic front. Credit on UPI is the frontier waiting to be unlocked. Contextual lending could genuinely change spending power for first-time borrowers. When commerce becomes more fluid, the economy becomes more productive.
Beyond that, there are three quieter shifts that are worth watching. The first, I expect, will be conversational, AI-led payments that let people transact in the language they already think in.
The next one that comes to mind is the extension of this power of payments to the offline world, to places the internet is yet to penetrate. And then comes the biggest change - programmable money that lets payments execute themselves when their conditions are met.
Smart-contract-like rules could automate conditional payments, while machine-to-machine and IoT micro-payments are already allowing devices, vehicles and software agents to pay one another securely in real time. This is bound to get more sophisticated. Maybe your fridge will order and pay for your groceries. If built with the same principles of interoperability, trust and inclusion, these innovations will not merely add features to UPI, but will expand what financial infrastructure can do for India, and increasingly, the world.
Ten years in, UPI’s real achievement won’t be the volumes, staggering as they are. It will be that an entire generation of Indians now expect their financial lives to simply work—instantly, safely, and without friction. I suspect the next decade will be about proving that India can build that same expectation into everything else it touches.
(Ambarish Kenghe is the Group Chief Executive Officer at Angel One )
(Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of YourStory.)

articles.title: Apple inaugure M6, la puce des prochains Macbook : qu'est-ce qui change ?
articles.text:
Depuis le M1 de novembre 2020, Apple déroule à peu près la même partition : une puce de base d’abord, puis les déclinaisons Pro, Max et Ultra qui suivent au fil des mois. Le M6 présenté ce mardi 25 août rompt avec cette routine, puisqu’il arrive seul (les versions musclées attendraient le M7, si les rumeurs disent vrai). Et il a vocation à voyager, du Mac mini dès aujourd’hui au MacBook Pro d’entrée de gamme et à l’iMac pressentis pour l’automne, avant le MacBook Air et l’iPad Pro évoqués pour 2027.
Où sont passés les gros cœurs du M6 ?
Sur le papier, le M6 gagne deux cœurs de processeur par rapport au M5, douze contre dix. Le détail de la répartition raconte autre chose : deux cœurs « super », quatre cœurs « performance » et six cœurs « efficience », là où le M5 alignait quatre gros cœurs et six petits. Autrement dit, Apple a divisé par deux le nombre de ses cœurs les plus puissants sur sa puce grand public. Le vide est comblé par une catégorie intermédiaire apparue en mars sur les M5 Pro et M5 Max (où elle remplaçait purement et simplement les cœurs efficience).
Pour se représenter la brigade, pensez à une cuisine de restaurant : deux chefs pour les plats compliqués, quatre cuisiniers qui abattent le gros du service en consommant moins, six commis pour les corvées de fond (mises à jour en arrière-plan, indexation de vos fichiers). Le vocabulaire a changé en cours de route : les cœurs « super » du M6 sont les cœurs « performance » du M5 rebaptisés au printemps. Les nouveaux « performance », présentés comme inédits, ressemblent surtout à des cœurs efficience remis en forme. Les processeurs de smartphones fonctionnent depuis des années avec trois étages de cœurs ; sur une puce M de base, c’est en tout cas une première.
Côté chiffres, Apple revendique pour ce cœur « super » « la performance monocœur la plus rapide du monde », un titre déjà décerné au M5 Pro en mars. Elle annonce aussi 20 % de mieux en multicœur face au M5, avec deux cœurs de plus pour y parvenir. La comparaison avec le M1 (2,4 fois plus rapide, nous dit-on) fait joli dans un communiqué, mais elle mesure surtout six ans d’écart dans la gravure. Aucun chiffre, en revanche, sur la vitesse d’un seul cœur face au M5, la comparaison qui aurait vraiment compté. L’explication la plus plausible tient à la surface de silicium. Un cœur « super » est énorme, la gravure en 2 nm coûte cher, et quatre cœurs moyens rendent probablement plus de services par millimètre carré que deux gros de plus. Les tests indépendants trancheront, surtout sur les logiciels qui n’exploitent que trois ou quatre cœurs.
Deux Neural Engine, pour quoi faire ?
Le Neural Engine, ce bloc de la puce réservé aux calculs d’intelligence artificielle, a longtemps été le parent pauvre des fiches techniques. Seize cœurs sur le M1 de 2020, seize sur le M5, seize encore sur les M5 Pro et M5 Max ; seul l’Ultra en cumule trente-deux, grâce à ses deux puces Max accolées. Le M6 en embarque deux exemplaires de seize cœurs, soit trente-deux au total, autant que le M5 Ultra du Mac Studio et deux fois plus que le M5 Max des MacBook Pro haut de gamme. Apple promet le double de puissance de calcul de pointe par rapport à la génération précédente. Les couches logicielles du système répartissent d’elles-mêmes le travail entre les deux blocs, sans que les applications aient à s’en mêler.
Ce cerveau bis a un client tout désigné : Apple Intelligence. Derrière lui, Core AI, la boîte à outils présentée en juin aux développeurs à la WWDC, fait tourner des modèles en local sur le processeur, la puce graphique et le Neural Engine. Modèles maison d’Apple, génération d’images, retouche photo, rédaction assistée : tout ce qui transite par cette couche logicielle profitera des deux blocs. En France, le bénéfice se fera sentir sur les fonctions Apple Intelligence déjà disponibles en français. Siri AI, la vedette de macOS 27, débutera pour sa part en bêta et en anglais avant de s’étendre à d’autres langues.
Si votre idée de l’IA locale ressemble plutôt à LM Studio, Ollama ou un modèle Meta téléchargé sur votre Mac, le Neural Engine vous concerne beaucoup moins. Ces outils s’appuient sur la puce graphique, et c’est là qu’interviennent les accélérateurs neuronaux glissés dans chacun des douze cœurs GPU (Apple annonce près de 30 % de calcul IA en plus face au M5, dont une bonne partie vient mécaniquement des deux cœurs supplémentaires). Pensez au Neural Engine comme à une voie réservée : rapide, mais ouverte aux seuls véhicules munis du bon badge, ceux qui passent par Core AI. Le reste du trafic emprunte la route principale.
Et sur cette route principale, le goulet d’étranglement s’appelle bande passante mémoire. Pour produire chaque mot (chaque token, pour les puristes), un modèle de langage relit l’intégralité de ses paramètres, un peu comme si vous deviez relire tout un livre avant d’en prononcer le mot suivant : la vitesse de lecture fait tout. Le M6 monte à 170 Go/s, soit 10 % de mieux que le M5 et environ 40 % de plus que le M4. De quoi éclairer la promesse d’Apple sur le Mac mini, annoncé quatre fois plus rapide en IA que son prédécesseur M4. Le seul exemple chiffré côté IA, 4,8 fois plus rapide dans LM Studio, mesure la lecture de votre question ; la vitesse à laquelle la réponse s’affiche, elle, suit la bande passante. Quant à la mémoire, le M6 plafonne à 32 Go, comme le M4 en 2024 et le M5 en 2025 : trois générations au même mur, sur une puce qu’Apple destine, entre autres, aux « passionnés d’IA ».
Le vrai cadeau du 2 nm ira aux MacBook et à l’iPad
Reste la gravure, l’argument que le communiqué d’Apple place en tête de gondole. Le M6 est la première puce Apple gravée en 2 nm, avec quelques semaines d’avance sur l’A20 attendu dans les iPhone 18 Pro de septembre (si le calendrier habituel tient). Sur le papier, le 2 nm de TSMC (le fondeur taïwanais qui fabrique toutes les puces Apple) promet 10 à 15 % de performance en plus à consommation égale face au 3 nm précédent. Ou 25 à 30 % de consommation en moins à performance égale, ce qui intéresse davantage un portable qu’un boîtier de bureau comme le Mac Mini. Le M5 reposant déjà sur une version améliorée de ce 3 nm, l’écart réel sera un peu plus faible. Ces chiffres viennent du fondeur ; Apple, de son côté, ne communique aucune donnée sur l’efficacité énergétique de son M6.
Le premier Mac à recevoir le M6 est un Mac mini, une machine qui n’a jamais eu à surveiller sa batterie, ce qui explique sans doute cette discrétion sur l’énergie. L’autonomie, la chauffe, le silence des ventilateurs (ou leur absence pure et simple), tout ce que le 2 nm peut apporter de plus tangible se jugera sur un MacBook Pro, Air ou un iPad Pro. Ces deux machines n’existent pas encore en M6 et ne devraient pas arriver avant 2027. Le communiqué prend soin de préciser que le 2 nm permet de loger davantage de transistors dans une puce plus petite. Plus petite, donc moins chère à fabriquer, ce qui renvoie à nos deux cœurs « super » disparus.
