articles.title: Tiny robots powered by light can hunt down and collect bacteria
articles.text:
Tiny robots powered by light can hunt down and collect bacteria
Light-powered nanorobots can now hunt down, collect, and relocate bacteria like futuristic microscopic cleaning crews.
- Date:
- August 18, 2026
- Source:
- University of Würzburg
- Summary:
- Researchers have built microscopic, light-driven robots that can rapidly navigate through liquid, collect bacteria, and deposit them in chosen locations. These tiny “cleaners” could open new possibilities for manipulating cells and microbes with remarkable precision.
- Share:
Robots small enough to operate in the microbial world could give scientists a new way to directly handle objects that are impossible to manipulate by hand. These tiny machines are around 50 times smaller than the diameter of a human hair, bringing researchers closer to the long-pursued goal of interacting directly with the microscopic world.
That capability could be especially useful for biological materials in water, including individual cells and bacteria. Precisely controlling and moving objects at this scale has been a persistent challenge. The newly developed nanorobots show that it is already possible to collect bacteria, transport them, and release them at selected locations.
Light Powers and Steers the Tiny Robots
One of the biggest obstacles in developing machines this small is finding an effective way to propel and control them. At Julius-Maximilians-Universität Würzburg (JMU), a research team led by Professor Bert Hecht has been developing a solution that uses the recoil produced by individual photons to move microscopic devices known as microdrones.
The devices contain as many as four plasmonic nanoantennas. These antennas absorb light with a particular color and helicity, then emit that light in a specific direction. Redirecting each photon creates a tiny recoil force, similar in principle to the recoil produced when a bullet is fired. Because the microdrones have so little mass, those extremely small forces can generate substantial acceleration and speed.
For the latest work, the researchers reduced the size of their light-powered robots even further, producing devices smaller than one micrometer. Simplifying the steering system was an important part of achieving that size while retaining propulsion based on photon recoil.
The new control method takes advantage of nanoscale antenna wires built into the robot. These wires naturally tend to align with the polarization direction of incoming light. By changing the light's polarization, the researchers can control which direction the nanorobot faces. At the same time, photon recoil continues to propel it forward, creating a steering system that works somewhat like the directional control used in larger vehicles.
Nanorobots Act as "Microscopic Cleaners"
"In essence, we have built a light-driven nanorobot that can track down and collect bacteria," says Jin Qin, lead experimental scientist of the study. "By simplifying the design, we reached a size at which these robots can operate directly in the microbial world - almost like microscopic cleaning devices."
The robots are also highly maneuverable. They can make extremely fast 90° turns, helping them scan broad areas of a sample in an organized and efficient way. They can also selectively capture, carry, and release substantial numbers of bacteria.
Under controlled laboratory conditions, this means the nanorobots can effectively "clean" microscopic environments. They gather bacteria from one area and deposit them at specifically chosen locations.
"This is a striking example of how light can be used not only to observe the microscopic world, but also to actively shape it," adds Bert Hecht. "The idea of tiny robotic cleaners may sound futuristic, but we are already demonstrating the physical principles that make it possible."
The robots remain fully maneuverable even while carrying larger groups of bacteria, although their speed decreases somewhat under the added load. That ability to keep functioning while transporting larger bacterial clusters points to possible future uses in microbiology, biomedical research, and precise manipulation of materials at the microscopic scale.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Würzburg. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Jin Qin, Carsten Büchner, Xiaofei Wu, Bert Hecht. A nanoscale robotic cleaner. Nature Communications, 2026; 17 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-70685-9

articles.title: En 2006, lanzaron un Boeing 737 al fondo del Pacífico. 20 años después, la vida marina lo ha convertido en un arrecife artificial
articles.text:
El 14 de enero de 2006, una grúa bajó lentamente un Boeing 737-200 retirado hasta las aguas del estrecho de Georgia, frente a Chemainus, en la isla canadiense de Vancouver. No había sufrido ningún accidente: sus propietarios querían que terminara en el fondo del mar. Casi veinte años después, aquel fuselaje vacío se ha transformado en un hábitat colonizado por numerosas especies marinas y en uno de los pecios de buceo más peculiares de la costa del Pacífico canadiense.
Historia de 737. El avión se construyó en 1975 y pasó por las flotas de Pacific Western Airlines, Canadian Airlines y finalmente Air Canada, acumulando más de 73.000 horas de vuelo antes de que fuera retirado en 2001 debido a su edad y problemas estructurales.
Posteriormente, Qwest Air Parts adquirió el aparato para aprovechar sus componentes y en el aeropuerto de Vancouver se retiraron motores, tren de aterrizaje y otras piezas reutilizables. El fuselaje terminó en manos de la Artificial Reef Society of British Columbia (ARSBC), después de que en 2002 surgiera la idea de darle una segunda vida muy diferente: convertir un antiguo avión de pasajeros en una estructura sobre la que pudiera instalarse vida marina.
No bastaba con tirarlo al mar. El proyecto necesitó casi cuatro años de preparativos y cientos de horas de trabajo voluntario antes de recibir luz verde. Se eliminaron grasa, aislamiento y cualquier material que pudiera contaminar el océano, se limpiaron cuidadosamente las superficies y se practicaron aberturas para facilitar tanto la colonización marina como el paso seguro de los buceadores.
También hubo que encontrar un emplazamiento adecuado y obtener permisos de Environment Canada y de seis comunidades de las Primeras Naciones antes de decidir que el Boeing terminaría frente a Chemainus, unos 70 kilómetros al norte de Victoria.
La grúa y el fondo del mar. El avión, de unos 30 metros de longitud, se colocó en posición vertical sobre unos soportes de 3,3 metros que lo mantienen separado del fondo, permitiendo que animales y buceadores puedan pasar también por debajo del fuselaje. La profundidad máxima del lugar ronda los 27 metros, mientras que buena parte del fuselaje se encuentra aproximadamente a 21 metros bajo la superficie.
De hecho, los buceadores pueden atravesar la antigua cabina de pasajeros, asomarse a las bodegas de carga y avanzar hasta una cabina de vuelo donde ya no hay pilotos: ahora son pequeños peces los que encuentran refugio en ella.
20 años después, el acero se cubre de vida. ¿Qué ocurrió? Que con el paso de los años, las superficies desnudas del Boeing empezaron a ser colonizadas por organismos marinos hasta convertir aquella carcasa industrial en un hábitat submarino. En el entorno del avión se han documentado peces de roca, lingcod, juveniles que utilizan la estructura como refugio, esponjas, anémonas plumosas, estrellas pluma, pulpos, pepinos de mar y erizos rojos.
El arrecife recibió precisamente el nombre Xihuw, término hul'qumi'num para los erizos rojos que antiguamente abundaban en estas aguas y cuyas poblaciones habían disminuido por la contaminación y la sobrepesca.
No basta con hundir cualquier cosa. Qué duda cabe, el Xihuw ilustra por qué barcos, aviones y otras estructuras pueden proporcionar superficies, escondites y nuevos espacios para organismos marinos, pero la ciencia advierte de que el resultado depende y mucho del lugar, la profundidad y el diseño. La razón: aunque los arrecifes artificiales pueden albergar comunidades de peces comparables a las de estructuras naturales e incluso funcionar como puntos intermedios para la dispersión de algunas especies, no son una solución automática para recuperar un ecosistema degradado.
En este caso, hubo años de planificación, descontaminación y selección del emplazamiento antes de que el Boeing tocara el agua. Desde entonces, la naturaleza lleva casi dos décadas encargándose de transformar un avión que recorrió los cielos de Canadá en un pequeño ecosistema del Pacífico.

articles.title: AI models flub these intelligence tests. Can you fare any better?
articles.text:
AI models flub these intelligence tests. Can you fare any better?
Puzzles and games can reveal gaps in models’ smarts. Try your hand at these seven tests to see if you can outwit AI.
Puzzles and games have been central to AI development since the very beginning. Just as we humans like to test our smarts with crosswords or logic puzzles, developers can test how far models have advanced with a gaming gauntlet. The term “machine learning” was popularized in a 1959 article by the IBM computer scientist Arthur Samuel about an algorithm that learned to play checkers. Chess and the Chinese board game Go are famous AI test beds too.
Judged purely on its puzzling skills, AI is improving a lot—and quickly. In late 2024, a team of scientists from Columbia University showed that even the best models could figure out only 18% of the infamous New York Times Connections puzzles; by early 2025, some models could solve them near perfectly every time.
But puzzles do more than just highlight the inexorable advance of AI capabilities. Seeing where models succeed and fail—and where we humans still beat them—can provide a useful window into the technology’s strengths and weaknesses. Despite advances, today’s models still fumble: Subtle changes in classic riddles often trip them up, and visual puzzles are a particular weak spot.
Here you’ll have the chance to test your wits on puzzles that have stumped models at one time or another. Some might be as tricky for you as they were for the AI; others are so simple that they’ll have you doubting whether AI is really intelligent at all. Each one highlights at least one way in which machine and human cognition differ. If you ace the test, you’ll have proved that you can out-puzzle an AI—at least for now.
Spatial Reasoning
Let’s start with a domain where humans have a huge advantage: spatial reasoning. If you’ve ever taken an IQ test, you may have done a mental rotation problem. These puzzles ask you to determine whether different images represent the same objects from different angles. Though today’s language models typically have the ability to analyze visual inputs, they still fail abysmally at these puzzles. For all the talk of how world models can help AI understand physical environments, LLMs still don’t seem to be able to manipulate 3D objects the way spatial thinkers like architects and mechanical engineers can.
Mental Rotation
Instructions: Choose the answer that shows the object in the prompt, but from a different angle. In each case, there’s only one correct answer!
Memory & Adaptability
Frontier LLMs have extraordinary memories; they were exposed to a monstrous volume of facts during training and can recite many of them faithfully. That’s an asset for outcompeting humans at trivia, but it can also be a liability. When a puzzle closely resembles one a model saw during training, the model may whiz by key differences and respond with what it memorized.
This held true in a 2024 study in which researchers from Google and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign trained and tested models on slight variations of a classic type of puzzle called Knights and Knaves. In these problems, some characters always tell the truth and others always lie, and you have to figure out who’s who. The same principle may be at work in a test called SimpleBench. These questions resemble more complicated problems that models likely encountered in training. Humans spot the trick, but even top-tier models trip.
Knights and Knaves
Instructions: The only thing you need to know to solve these puzzles is that knights always tell the truth and knaves always lie. Determine who’s what on the basis of what each character says.
                    You have met a group of two islanders.
                    
                    Their names are Edward and Wallace.
                
                Wallace says: Edward tells the truth.
Edward says: Wallace and I are the same type.
                    You have met a group of three islanders.
                    
                    Their names are Joseph, Francine, and Alice.
                
                Francine says: Joseph is a knave.
Francine says: Alice tells the truth.
Alice says: Joseph is not my type.
                    You have met a group of three islanders.
                    
                    Their names are Robert, Vincent, and Michelle.
                
                Michelle says: Robert always lies.
Vincent says: Michelle is truthful.
Robert says: Vincent is untruthful.
Robert says: Vincent is not my type.
SimpleBench
Instructions: Read these SimpleBench problems carefully, and you should be able to figure out the answers in no time.
Beth places four whole ice cubes in a frying pan at the start of the first minute, then five at the start of the second minute and some more at the start of the third minute, but none in the fourth minute. If the average number of ice cubes per minute placed in the pan while it was frying a crispy egg was five, how many whole ice cubes can be found in the pan at the end of the third minute?
A juggler throws a solid blue ball a meter in the air and then a solid purple ball (of the same size) two meters in the air. She then climbs to the top of a tall ladder carefully, balancing a yellow balloon on her head. Where is the purple ball most likely now, in relation to the blue ball?
Abstract & Visual Reasoning
AI doesn’t just bungle visual problems in 3D—two dimensions can trip it up as well. That’s a major factor in how well models do on the most famous puzzle-based benchmark, ARC-AGI. These problems require you to infer abstract, general rules from a set of examples. Models do better on ARC puzzles when they receive each grid not as an image but as a string of numbers that encodes the color of each cell.
Research suggests that even when models answer ARC-AGI questions correctly, they often do so using byzantine and non-generalizable rules, whereas humans draw on simple visual concepts. Despite these disadvantages, models have gotten quite good at ARC-AGI over the past year, but some puzzles—such as the one printed here—still stump them.
ARC-AGI
Instructions: Study the three pairs of grids shown below to figure out the rule that dictates how the ones on the left transform into the ones on the right. Then get out your markers or colored pencils and fill in the fourth grid using that rule. (The solution is the same no matter which way the grids are oriented.)
Pair 1
Pair 2
Pair 3
Now you try it
Puzzle
Your answer
Intuition
It’s not just AI models that fall into traps. We humans have our own cognitive foibles, many of which AI does not share. Psychologists have designed problem suites that invert the SimpleBench phenomenon: For these questions, humans often give knee-jerk answers, whereas models will respond deliberatively. Some of the problems exploit errors in the ways that we intuitively do math; others are phrased so as to suggest obvious answers that fall apart if the question is read carefully.
Lightning Round
Instructions: Answer the questions below as quickly as you can.
In a cave, there is a colony of bats whose population doubles each day. Given that it takes 60 days for the entire cave to be filled with bats, how many days would it take for the cave to be half-filled with bats?
In what famous novel does Alice state "I'm late, I'm late, for a very important date"?
Increasing Complexity
In some cases, whether an LLM can complete a puzzle is a matter of scale. One study from researchers at Apple found that LLMs can ace simple versions of the Tower of Hanoi problem, which involves moving a stack of disks one at a time without ever putting a larger disk atop a smaller one, and river-crossing puzzles, in which a group of people must traverse a river according to certain rules. But only up to a point: As the number of disks or people hits six and higher, the models began to falter.
In another study, researchers at the University of Washington, Stanford University, and the Allen Institute for AI observed that LLMs struggle similarly with logic grid puzzles, which require deducing the attributes of a set of individuals from a list of clues. The Apple paper went viral, but commentators questioned whether the results reveal a unique limitation of LLM reasoning—or just that it’s normal to make errors as complexity piles up.
The River
Instructions: Using the scenario provided, plan the trips necessary to get everyone across the river.
Three FBI agents and their three informants need to cross a river. They have a rowboat that can fit only two people, though it can be rowed by only one. Each agent will refuse to leave their informant on the same bank as other agents without them present—even if the informant never steps out of the boat and onto the bank. How can all six make it across?
Logic Grid
Instructions: Using the list of clues, determine who lives in each house and what style of music each person enjoys. There is only one possible solution. You may find it helpful to fill out the grid below to keep track of your deductions.
The Neighborhood
- There are 4 houses, numbered 1 to 4 from left to right, as seen from across the street.
- Each house is occupied by a different person: Peter, Eric, Arnold, or Alice.
- Each resident has a favorite type of music: jazz, rock, classical, or pop.
- Alice is directly left of Peter.
- The person who loves classical music is directly left of Peter.
- Arnold loves jazz music.
- The person who loves rock music is not in the second house.
- The person who loves rock music is directly left of the person who loves pop music.
Click a cell to mark an X, click again for a check mark.
Grace Huckins is an AI reporter at MIT Technology Review. They have a PhD in neuroscience.

articles.title: On a vu The Dog Stars, le nouveau Ridley Scott et c'est décevant
articles.text:
Adapté du roman éponyme de Peter Heller paru en 2012, The Dog Stars est déjà le trentième long-métrage de Ridley Scott ! Le cinéaste britannique a en effet débuté sa carrière à la fin des années 70. On lui doit des chefs-d’œuvre cinématographiques comme Alien, Blade Runner, Thelma et Louise ou encore Gladiator pour ne citer qu’eux.
Quand on est aussi prolifique, il y a nécessairement quelques ratés. La carrière de Ridley Scott s’avère inégale et ses derniers films, notamment Napoléon ou Gladiator 2, n’ont pas toujours convaincu. Avec The Dog Stars, le réalisateur revient à l’un de ses genres favoris, l’anticipation, tout en dépouillant un maximum l’univers. Exit les mondes compliqués d’Alien ou Blade Runner, celui de The Dog Stars se veut réaliste. Il prend d’ailleurs place en 2035, autant dire demain !
On y suit l’histoire de Hig (Jacob Elordi), un jeune pilote mécanicien qui survit dans l’État du Colorado avec son chien, Jasper, dans un monde post-apocalyptique où l’humanité a été ravagée par un virus.
Son quotidien est fait de sorties à bord de son vieux coucou, un monomoteur Cessna 182 avec lequel il sillonne la région, se ravitaille et aide une communauté de mennonites (des chrétiens évangéliques pacifiques). Il vit sur une ancienne base aérienne, qu’il défend des intrus hostiles avec Bangley (Josh Brolin), un vieux de la vieille tendance survivaliste. Hig espère qu’il existe un endroit où il pourrait être plus heureux…
Nature et Découverte
S’il trouve sa source dans un best-seller, le pitch de The Dog Stars se révèle assez générique pour un film post-apocalyptique ! Les premières images du monde imaginé par Ridley Scott le confirment. Ces infrastructures et villes laissées à l’abandon, sur lesquelles la nature a repris ses droits, on les a déjà vues dans pléthore d’œuvres post-apo, de Je suis une légende à la franchise sérielle The Walking Dead.
La petite nouveauté ici, c’est que Hig a le loisir de sillonner les alentours à bord de son avion brinquebalant, ce qui donne lieu à des plans de la nature vue du ciel, assez époustouflants. Cela apporte au film une dimension contemplative agréable. Mais la nature, aussi sublimée soit-elle ici, ne fait pas un blockbuster à elle toute seule.
The Dog Stars s’inscrit dans la lignée d’un sous-genre cinématographique non-officiel assez tendance ces derniers temps, les films qu’on appelera « un homme et son chien ». Récemment, L’appel de la forêt avec Harrison Ford et bientôt Heart of the Beast porté par Brad Pitt viennent s’ajouter à une liste déjà longue de films centrés sur la relation entre un personnage masculin bourru et son compagnon à quatre pattes. De son côté, Ridley Scott a misé sur un des chefs de file de la nouvelle génération d’acteurs hollywoodiens, Jacob Elordi.
Le héros d’action, version Gen Z
Révélé par la série Euphoria et le teen movie Kissing Booth, Jacob Elordi s’est depuis illustré dans des films centrés sur des romances comme Priscilla de Sofia Coppola ou Saltburn et Hurlevent, deux films signés Emerald Fennell. Sa récente prestation dans le Frankenstein de Guillermo Del Toro a été remarquée et lui avait permis de dévoiler une autre facette de son jeu d’acteur.
Avec The Dog Stars, il accède à un rôle principal dans un film qui contient un bon nombre de scènes d’action. Et il assure dans ce nouveau registre, tout en apportant une vulnérabilité dans sa performance (par exemple, Hig pleure dans le film) qui permet de renouveler l’archétype du héros insubmersible (incarné ici par le toujours très cool Josh Brolin en second rôle).
Hig est un vrai gentil, un homme hanté par la mort de sa femme, dont l’humeur oscille entre espoir de reconstruire une vie plaisante et pensées suicidaires. Ridley Scott, qui a perdu son frère (le cinéaste Tony Scott s’est suicidé en 2012) explore sans doute ici des thématiques intimes. On passe en tout cas volontiers le film en compagnie de Hig, ainsi qu’en celle de Margaret Qualley, qui arrive un peu plus tard dans le récit dans le rôle de Cima, une jeune femme vivant isolée avec son père (le revenant Guy Pearce) qui va lui redonner une raison de vivre.
L’aspect intimiste du film et la trajectoire personnelle de Hig, le besoin de faire son deuil de sa vie passée, sont traités de façon classique mais efficace. On se prend d’affection pour cet embryon (Hig, Cima, son père et Bangley) de famille recomposée. Reste que la comparaison avec la plus moderne et inventive série The Last of Us plane au-dessus des têtes de The Dog Stars…
Rien de nouveau sous le soleil post-apo
S’il y a un domaine dans lequel le savoir-faire de Ridley Scott reste indéniable, c’est la mise en scène de séquences d’action spectaculaires. Le film réserve ainsi plusieurs scènes haletantes et explosives, durant lesquelles Hig et ses compagnons d’infortune font face à divers antagonistes, aux allures quasiment zombiesques.
Mention spéciale à celle durant laquelle Bangley affronte, tel un personnage de jeu vidéo, une violente horde humaine en pleine nuit, armé de sa vision infrarouge. On passe un moment plaisant devant ce blockbuster, mais il s’avère trop prévisible pour marquer durablement les esprits.
Ridley Scott a tendance à se reposer sur des poncifs hollywoodiens qu’il évitait dans le passé : la femme morte pour donner de la profondeur au héros, le love interest féminin entouré d’hommes qui est là pour les soigner et /ou les consoler ou encore une tribu qui attaque à cheval avec des peintures de guerre, évoquant l’imaginaire « occidentalo-colonial » des westerns américains… Le film propose un univers très manichéen : en sous-texte, on comprend que seuls nos héros savent apparemment comment « bien » faire communauté, de façon civilisée.
Tout cela pour arriver à une conclusion universelle – faire communauté est encore la meilleure manière d’exister – illustrée par une séquence tout droit sortie du reboot de La Petite Maison dans la prairie ! Cette scène résonne avec la toute fin d’Euphoria, qui nous laissait en compagnie d’une famille d’évangéliques.
Les réalisateurs américains ne semblent avoir qu’une seule réponse au monde dans lequel ils vivent sous l’ère Trump : revenir à un patriarcat chrétien et pré-capitaliste, comme si c’était la réponse à tous nos maux contemporains. Et si la fiction, comme Ridley Scott lui-même a su le faire dans le passé, nous proposait d’autres imaginaires, plus novateurs, plus désirables ? C’est peut-être la tâche qui revient à la prochaine génération de cinéastes.
En attendant, Ridley Scott, 88 ans, n’imaginera pas le monde de demain, mais il s’amuse avec celui d’hier : il est déjà en train de préparer son prochain projet, un remake de L’île au trésor.
Le verdict
The Dog Stars
Voir la fiche
On a aimé
- Jacob Elordi convaincant en héros d’action, nouvelle génération
- Des scènes d’action efficaces
- Une vraie dimension contemplative
On a moins aimé
- Manque d’originalité général
- Un imaginaire daté et parfois discutable
- Un film trop sage pour du post-apo

articles.title: "Europe is aging rapidly": Solace Care raises €2.1 million in largest pre-Seed round to date for a European end-of-life platform | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Solace Care, a Stockholm-based end-of-life platform, has raised a pre-Seed round of €2.1 million to expand its insurer and broker partnerships, enter the Netherlands and the UK, and grow its product and commercial teams.
The round was led by Spintop Ventures, with participation from Plug and Play, alongside Caroline Farberger (former CEO of ICA Försäkring), Fredrik Solberg (former CEO of Eir Insurance), Emil Lagerstedt-Karlsson (former VP Insurance & Insurtech at Insurely), Tomi Yli-Kyyny (former CEO of Fennia) and Stefan Moritz (former Head of Innovation at Max Matthiessen), together with Further Than Capital, Mattias Miksche, Krim Talia and Wave Ventures.
“Today, insurance pays out and then the family is on their own for the next six months,” says Valtteri Korkiakoski, CEO and co-founder of Solace Care. “We are redefining personal insurance, so the support is not only a payment. It should help the family keep going.”
As per EU-Startups coverage, Solace Care’s pre-Seed round lands amid continued European investment in insurance technology and digitally delivered care in 2026.
Over the past year, we have seen more than €199 million across a selection of adjacent rounds, including over €25 million for Copenhagen-based Festina Finance to modernise life-insurance and pension infrastructure, €42.2 million for UK InsurTech mea Platform, €20.1 million for Serbian-Hungarian insurer Ominimo, and €11 million for Frankfurt-based Oska Health, whose digital care model is distributed through health insurers.
In Sweden, Stockholm-based pet InsurTech Lassie raised €63.2 million to expand its prevention-led insurance model across Europe, providing a same-country comparison, albeit in a different insurance category.
“Life insurance has been sold on the same promise for decades,” adds Erik Wenngren, Partner at Spintop Ventures. “Solace Care changes what the product actually delivers to a family, both before and after a loss. That is rare in this industry, and the team has the operating history to execute it.”
Solace Care was founded in 2025 by Valtteri Korkiakoski and Josef Karakoca, a founding pair who previously helped build and scale Mindler, a digital healthcare company.
Sold through life insurers and brokers, Solace Care is a digital platform for legacy planning and support after loss. It helps users put their affairs in order while they still can, and guides their families through the practical and emotional work that follows a death.
Before a loss, policyholders use Solace Care to record their wishes, gather documents, and leave clear instructions – a vault they can share with family, extending coverage from the insured individual to the people who will actually do the work. After a loss, the family is guided through the practical administration, institution by institution, with human support alongside the platform.
Solace Care went from its first policyholders in mid-2025 to more than 25,000 covered lives across Sweden, Finland and Norway.
“A year ago we had zero covered lives,” says Valtteri. “The growth has not come from marketing. It has come from partners who put our solution in front of their customers and saw the positive response to the product.”
The service is available today in Swedish, Finnish, Norwegian with on-going plans to scale into the Danish and Dutch markets.
“A product that does nothing for you until you die is a tough sell to a healthy 35-year-old,” says Josef. “Put planning and support around it and the same policy suddenly does something for the family right now, not just after loss. Thatʼs the value weʼre building.ˮ
The capital will build out enterprise sales capability: deepening existing Nordic carrier and broker partnerships, opening the Netherlands and the UK, where Solace Care has already appointed local commercial advisors, and adding senior hires in product and commercial operations.
“Europe is aging rapidly, and no European player owns this end-of-life space yet,” says Korkiakoski. “We will change the way we think about death and insurance.“

articles.title: IBM is building a dual-architecture mainframe chip that will run Arm and Z software on the same cores
articles.text:
First look: IBM is developing a mainframe chip designed to run Arm software directly alongside IBM Z and LinuxONE code. The approach could let customers add Linux, cloud and AI applications while keeping core transaction workloads on the same system.
The processor was showcased at Hot Chips 2026 and is expected to use 11 IBM Z cores built on a 2-nanometer process. IBM said the cores will operate above 5.7 GHz and support native execution of both z/Architecture and AArch64 instructions.
That's the central change here: IBM isn't placing separate Arm and Z cores on the same chip, and it isn't using emulation. Instead, Arm instruction support is being built directly into the mainframe core, with each processor core able to run Arm instructions concurrently with IBM Z or LinuxONE instructions.
The design could make it easier for customers to run Arm-based Linux, cloud-native and AI software alongside mainframe applications that handle core transaction and database workloads. IBM said it wants to combine the reach of the Arm software ecosystem with the scalability, security and high-availability features associated with Z and LinuxONE.
The chip will also include a set of specialized accelerators. IBM plans AI inference hardware for in-transaction fraud detection, a data processing unit for I/O acceleration, and separate accelerators for compression, cryptography and sorting.
Its cache system is substantial: IBM disclosed a 36 MB private L2 cache, a 432 MB virtual L3 cache and as much as 3.5 GB of virtual L4 cache, resources intended to keep latency low for large databases and transaction-heavy workloads.
IBM hasn't named the processor or announced the system that will use it, but the company said it expects the design to arrive in 2028. IBM launched its current z17 mainframe generation in 2025 and has generally updated the platform on a three-year schedule, making the chip a likely candidate for a future z18 family.
The announcement comes as Arm gains a larger role in enterprise infrastructure. Major cloud providers have introduced their own Arm processors, while open-source infrastructure, AI and cloud-native software increasingly supports the architecture. According to Meredith Stowell, IBM's vice president for the zSystems Ecosystem, the Arm ecosystem includes more than 22 million developers and a growing selection of cloud-native, AI, analytics, infrastructure and enterprise software.
IBM's mainframes remain central to many large organizations, particularly in financial services. IBM says its Z and LinuxONE systems run 68% of the world's production IT workloads, while 77 of the world's 100 largest banks use the platforms.
Still, the mainframe market is limited compared with the broader server market. That can make IBM Z a lower priority for independent software vendors, even as the systems continue to run some of the most critical workloads inside major companies.
George Cozma, an analyst at TechInsights, told The Register that the market is "small in unit terms" but "strategically important." He said customers rarely replace mainframes because "core applications, decades of operational practice, and data gravity make migration expensive and risky."
Cozma said the dual-architecture processor could help close the distance between IBM Z and the software environment driving modern cloud and AI deployments. The technology would let IBM retain the features that have long defined its mainframes while expanding the software available to customers.
IBM Z systems already run Linux workloads beside z/OS applications through KVM and OpenShift virtualization. The new processor would expand that model by supporting both s390x/Z and Arm64 virtual machines.
IBM hasn't announced plans to support operating systems beyond those discussed at Hot Chips. But by adding Arm execution directly to the processor, the company is trying to make its next mainframe generation more useful for organizations that need both legacy-scale transaction processing and newer Linux and AI workloads.

articles.title: SpaceX recupera Starship no oceano em operação inédita e inicia viagem de volta aos EUA
articles.text:
Uma operação inédita envolvendo a espaçonave Starship foi concluída com sucesso nas proximidades da Ilha Christmas, território australiano no Oceano Índico, a cerca de 500 km ao sul de Jacarta, capital da Indonésia.
Em publicação no X, Michal Václavík, especialista em astronáutica do Czech Space Office (CSO), órgão responsável por coordenar a participação da República Tcheca em atividades espaciais internacionais, confirmou que a Starship foi colocada com sucesso sobre o navio semissubmersível Forte (da operadora holandesa Boskalis). O procedimento representa um passo importante para a recuperação de veículos espaciais após voos de teste.
Starship (S40) je u břehů Vánočního ostrova nakládána (nyní asi již naložena) na poloponornou loď FORTE. Autorem snímků je australský fotograf Chris Bray. pic.twitter.com/Un2ZDGOpEX
— Michal Vaclavik (@Kosmo_Michal) August 26, 2026
A Ship 40, Starship utilizada na operação, participou do 13º voo de teste da SpaceX, realizado em 24 de julho. Após completar a missão, a espaçonave reentrou na atmosfera e fez um pouso controlado no Oceano Índico, onde permaneceu à deriva durante semanas.
Operação exigiu manobra complexa
Por mais de três semanas, equipes trabalharam para rebocar a Starship até uma região de águas mais tranquilas próxima à Ilha Christmas. O transporte exigiu cuidados especiais para evitar danos à estrutura da espaçonave durante a operação.
De acordo com a emissora australiana ABC, o Forte utilizou seus tanques de lastro para afundar parcialmente o convés. Com a embarcação submersa, a Starship, que tem cerca de 52 metros de comprimento, pôde ser posicionada sobre a estrutura.
Depois, os tanques foram esvaziados para que o navio voltasse a subir, elevando a espaçonave para fora da água. A manobra permitiu retirar o veículo do oceano sem a necessidade de desmontá-lo no local.
Mesmo após permanecer por semanas na água, a estrutura principal da Starship continuou preservada, o que fornecerá informações importantes para os engenheiros da SpaceX.
Incredible timelapse of the carrier ship Forte rising from the ocean with Starship 40 safely loaded on board at Christmas Island, Australia.
📸 Chris Bray Photography pic.twitter.com/VzCnWej8RP
Starship seguirá para o Texas
Agora, o Forte deve iniciar a travessia do Oceano Pacífico com a Starship a bordo rumo à Starbase, complexo da SpaceX localizado no Texas, nos Estados Unidos, a 17 mil km de distância.
Até o momento, não há qualquer comunicado oficial da SpaceX com previsão de chegada ao destino.
Quando isso acontecer, os componentes da espaçonave deverão passar por análises detalhadas. Entre os itens de maior interesse estão o sistema de proteção térmica, os motores e outras partes submetidas a condições extremas durante o voo.
Os dados obtidos podem ajudar a empresa a entender como a Starship se comporta após um voo completo e permanecer na água por um período prolongado. Essas informações também poderão contribuir para o desenvolvimento de versões futuras do veículo e para aumentar a segurança de missões cada vez mais complexas.
Flávia Correia é jornalista do Olhar Digital, cobrindo Ciência e Espaço.

articles.title: KI breitet sich im Internet aus: An wie vielen Seiten Agenten und Chatbots schon mitwirken
articles.text:
KI im Internet: Wie viele Seiten wurden von Chatbots und Agenten geschrieben?
Wer im Internet unterwegs ist, trifft schon lange nicht mehr nur auf Inhalte, die von Menschen erstellt wurden. Schon seit Jahrzehnten treiben auch Bots ihr Unwesen, aber erst in den vergangenen Jahren haben auch KI-Agenten und Chatbots ihre Wirkung auf das Internet entfaltet. So sehr, dass unter anderem Zukunftsforscherin Amy Webb davon ausgeht, dass das nächste Internet für Maschinen und nicht für Menschen geschaffen werden wird. Und erste Anzeichen dafür lassen sich heute schon erkennen.
KI-Inhalte im Netz: So viele Webseiten nutzen die Tools schon
Das geht aus einer Studie des Pew Research Centers mit dem Titel „How much of the internet is written with AI?“ hervor. Um herauszufinden, wie hoch der Anteil von KI-generierten Inhalten im Netz heute schon ist, haben sie Daten von Common Crawl genutzt. Das offene Repository stellt Daten von über 300 Milliarden Webseiten über knapp zwei Jahrzehnte bereit.
Für ihre Zwecke haben die Forscher:innen sich fast eine halbe Milliarde englischsprachige Webseiten der vergangenen fünf Jahre angeschaut. Dabei war ihnen wichtig, dass der Zeitraum auch die Zeit vor dem Release von ChatGPT beinhaltet. Im Anschluss wurden die Seiten durch das Tool Open Pangram gejagt, um herauszufinden, ob bei ihrer Erstellung KI genutzt wurde.
Das Ergebnis: Zehn Prozent aller analysierten Seiten zeigten „signifikante Anzeichen von KI-Autorenschaft“, wie es in der Studie heißt. Im ersten Moment mag das recht wenig klingen. Allerdings enthält dieser Datensatz noch die alten Webseiten, die vor dem ChatGPT-Release erstellt wurden. Entfernt man die Seiten aus der Internetanalyse, steigt der Anteil von Webseiten mit KI-generierten Inhalten auf 35 Prozent an.
Dabei betonen die Verantwortlichen, dass die Verteilung der Webseiten, die KI-generierte Inhalte nutzen, alles andere als gleichmäßig ist. Am häufigsten kommen KI-Inhalte bei englischsprachigen Webseiten auf .com-Domains vor. Sie machen knapp zehn Prozent aus. Danach folgen .org-Webseiten (4,6 Prozent). Mit jeweils einem Prozent sind .edu- und .gov-Seiten noch relativ KI-frei.

articles.title: Bose is resting on its laurels with its new headphones
articles.text:
Bose QuietComfort headphones used to be innovative. Bose’s noise-canceling research is the reason the technology is where it is today, and its headphones set the standard. They were the ubiquitous traveler’s accessory. But over the past few years, it’s felt like Bose has rested on that reputation, as other companies have caught up. Sony and Apple have both surpassed Bose in noise-canceling performance, and even midrange headphones like the $130 Soundcore Space 2 are close for much less money. That means the $359 Bose QuietComfort Headphones 2nd Gen need to stand out in other ways — and I don’t think they do.
The second-generation Bose QuietComfort Headphones are good, but don’t stand out
There’s nothing really wrong with the QuietComfort Headphones 2nd Gen, but there’s nothing exciting about them, either.
If you buy something from a Verge link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
The Good
- Great sound with minor tweaking
- Strong noise canceling
- Nice physical buttons
The Bad
- Call quality is still behind competitors
- No wireless high-res support
The second-generation Bose QuietComfort headphones look a lot like the QuietComfort Ultra Gen 2 that Bose launched last fall, but with more plastic instead of metal accents in the headband and joints. In addition to black and white, the QC Headphones come in mauve, a light avocado green, and a two-tone mint color, where the padding is darker than the rest of the headphones. The colors look nice, but headphones companies (including Bose) have been expanding on the reliable black and white options for years now, so colorful options are no longer novel.
The new QuietComfort Gen 2 are designed as a step-down model from the $449 Ultra Gen 2, but they’re slightly better in a few ways.
I usually find Bose headphones, including the Ultra Gen 2, to be bassy with a peaky high end, which the limited 3-band EQ in the app could never quite compensate for. But the default listening mode on the QC Gen 2 headphones is the best I’ve heard from Bose, and I think most people would be more than happy with the sound (I still prefer the stock sound from any of the Sony XM series). I do find the midrange muted, causing vocals to sound buried or snare hits — like at the beginning of The Cranberries’ “Zombie” — to lose their impact. But unlike on previous Bose headphones, I could fix the problem with the 3-band EQ in the app by boosting the mid to +4. It added more presence and settled in nicely between the bass and upper frequencies.
Bose built the QuietComfort line’s long-standing reputation on active noise cancellation. The Gen 2’s is solid, but not as strong as the flagship Ultra Headphones. I actually find that to be a good thing, though. I experience a phenomenon dubbed “eardrum suck” on the QC Ultra Headphones 2nd Gen because of their aggressive noise cancellation. It’s a disconcerting feeling that can feel like a change of pressure in your ears (although there’s no actual pressure change). I didn’t feel it with the QuietComfort Headphones, and while their noise-canceling performance isn’t quite as good as the Ultra’s, and certainly not as good as either the Sony XM6 or Apple AirPods Max 2 (which don’t cause eardrum suck for me, for some reason), it’s more than enough to block out airplane noise or AC units, especially when music is playing.
While the headphone jack is now gone, the USB-C connection supports both charging and audio (lossless up to 24-bit/48kHz), like the Ultra Gen 2. Bose also includes both a USB-C-to-USB-C and USB-C-to-3.5mm cable (color-matched to the headphones), so it’s still possible to connect to a 3.5mm source. But there’s no AptX Lossless or LDAC wireless high-res codec support (the Ultra Gen 2 support AptX Lossless, and LDAC is supported on a variety of headphones from Sony and others).
The QC Gen 2’s call quality is about the same as the Ultra Gen 2’s, and better than previous Bose headphones, but that’s a low bar. Bose still lags behind every major competitor and is light years behind the tech in Soundcore’s Liberty 5 Pro earbuds (which will likely come to its over-ear headphones soon). They add extra sibilance to my speaking voice and in loud environments compress the sound, which can cause sentences to clip, making me hard to understand.
Call quality aside, the Bose sound really good (especially with the midrange tweak), they have solid ANC performance, they’re light and relatively comfortable, and they have some nice color options. But the same can be said about the vast majority of headphones out there. There’s nothing about the Bose QuietComfort Headphones Gen 2 that really stands out, especially for $359.
Part of the problem is the price, which puts them in a no-man’s-land. Current-gen flagships like the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones 2nd Gen, Sony WH-1000XM6, and Apple AirPods Max 2 can be found on sale for $400 or a little more, while slightly older — but still competitive — headphones like the XM5 and Sennheiser Momentum 4 are often $250 or less.
That’s not to say the second-gen Bose QC Headphones are bad. Far from it. They’re a strong argument against spending the extra money on the Ultra Gen 2, but unless you want Bose headphones in particular, there’s not a compelling reason to get them. The $400 Sony WH-1000XM6 have better noise canceling, great call quality, and LDAC support, and I slightly prefer their stock sound. They even support Auracast with some phones. Apple’s AirPods Max 2 have a distinctive look and the same deep integration with Apple’s ecosystem as the AirPods Pro, and they can be found for as low as $430.
Give me a redesigned look. Give me high-res wireless support. Hell, give me Auracast. Give me any reason to say “the QuietComfort Headphones are the headphones to get” instead of just another iterative update. They aren’t bad headphones by any means, but Bose used to make the best ANC headphones. Now they’re just another pair that are good enough.
Photography by John Higgins / The Verge

articles.title: Lo nuevo de Instagram recorta y edita tus Reels con un toque y sin IA
articles.text:
Si editas tus Reels en el móvil, sabrás lo tedioso que puede llegar a ser. Dependiendo de tu nivel de "influencer", el proceso puede ir desde un simple ajuste en la app de Instagram o CapCut hasta otra herramienta externa. Meta ha decidido simplificar el proceso con First Draft (o primer borrador), una nueva función que ya está disponible en la app de Instagram.
De acuerdo con una publicación en su cuenta de Threads, First Draft puede cortar pausas y recortar los clips de forma automática con un solo toque. La herramienta analiza los vídeos que seleccionas y elimina los silencios para quedarte con lo más relevante. El resultado es un primer borrador del Reel, listo para que lo ajustes a tu gusto o lo publiques al momento.
Para usarlo solo necesitas grabar o seleccionar tus clips en la galería de Reels, tocar el botón de First Draft y esperar que la app haga el resto en cuestión de segundos. En caso de que tengas varios clips de más de un minuto cada uno, Instagram los analiza y detecta las partes con pausas largas o momentos muertos para descartarlos del corte final. Después de eso, la herramienta une los fragmentos seleccionados en un solo vídeo y permite una edición más a detalle, como reordenar escenas, eliminar partes o ajustar la duración.
También es posible empezar de cero si el resultado no te convence, ya que todos los cambios de First Draft se guardan en un borrador completamente editable. Esta herramienta funciona bien con distintos tipos de contenido, como montajes, vídeos tipo talking-head o publicaciones de día a día. El objetivo es ahorrarte el trabajo de recortar clip por clip para concentrarte en la parte creativa.
Instagram no usa IA en su nueva función First Draft
Por increíble que parezca, la nueva función de Instagram no utiliza inteligencia artificial. Esto es difícil de creer, sobre todo si consideramos que Meta está invirtiendo una cantidad indiscriminable de dinero para impulsar sus modelos en Meta AI. Sin embargo, este no es el caso, al menos en First Draft.
Nicole Rechtszaid, responsable de comunicación de Instagram, confirmó a The Verge que su sistema se basa en detección de pausas y silencios. A diferencia de Quick Cut de Adobe, que combina clips mediante indicaciones basadas en IA, la herramienta de Instagram opta por algo más tradicional. La compañía prefiere ocupar esos recursos de cómputo en otras funciones más indispensables dentro de sus otras aplicaciones.
Si quieres usar First Draft para crear tu primer borrador, solo necesitas abrir la cámara de Instagram y grabar tu vídeo (o seleccionar los clips). Posteriormente, basta tocar el botón ubicado en la parte inferior para esperar que IG haga su magia. Lamentablemente, esta función solo está disponible para iPhone y no se ha confirmado si llegará a Android en un futuro cercano.

articles.title: Instagram’s 'First Draft' feature aims to make editing Reels less tedious | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Instagram is making one of the most tedious parts of creating Reels easier. The company announced Tuesday in a Threads post that it’s rolling out “First Draft,” a new editing feature that automatically trims selected video clips and removes pauses, pulling together the best moments into an initial cut.
Instagram says the process can produce a first pass in under 10 seconds, potentially saving creators significant editing time while making video creation more approachable for people who don’t have much experience with editing software. Instead of manually working through every clip, creators can start with an automatically assembled draft and refine it from there.
First Draft is initially rolling out on iPhone. Users can access it directly from Instagram’s camera while recording or from the Reels gallery after selecting multiple clips.
The feature itself isn’t revolutionary. Similar automated editing tools already exist in products such as Adobe Firefly’s Quick Cuts and CapCut’s Auto Cut. But Instagram’s decision to build the functionality directly into its own app gives creators less reason to move footage into a separate editor.
Instagram has introduced several creator tools this year, such as a “Replace Audio” tool that lets users swap the music on existing feed posts and carousels without deleting and re-uploading them. The company is also working on launching a new AI assistant in its video-editing app Edits.
Additionally, it has been testing “Series,” which lets creators group related Reels together so viewers can watch them in a specific order, potentially turning individual short videos into more structured content.
Notably, First Draft was announced on the same day that Instagram head Adam Mosseri is expected to testify in Meta’s high-profile social media addiction trial. The lawsuit accuses Meta of designing Instagram and Facebook in ways that encouraged children to use the platforms compulsively while failing to address potential harms. Meta has rejected the allegations.

articles.title: 'We wanted to go out with a bang' — Geralt returns in The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt - Songs of the Past's new trailer, promising a final action-packed journey ahead of The Witcher 4
articles.text:
'We wanted to go out with a bang' — Geralt returns in The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt - Songs of the Past's new trailer, promising a final action-packed journey ahead of The Witcher 4
Is it 2027 yet?
- The first trailer for The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt - Songs of the Past has been revealed at Gamescom
- The trailer showcases Geralt, a new region, monsters, and a weapon
- CD Projekt Red level design lead Miles Tost confirms, "This is Geralt's last adventure before we pass the torch on to Ciri" in The Witcher 4
CD Projekt Red has unveiled the first look at The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt's third and final expansion, Songs of the Past, and it looks incredible.
Songs of the Past, which is being co-developed with Fool’s Theory, a studio whose leadership is made up of The Witcher 3 veterans, was revealed during Opening Night Live at Gamescom. While we still don't have a specific release date, the expansion's first trailer gave us a taste of what to look forward to.
We see Geralt of Rivia returning for a brand-new journey as he explores a new region, Letten, takes on creepy monsters, and wields a new chain weapon that can grapple enemies, first showcased in the first Witcher game.
CDPR Level design lead Miles Tost took to the stage during Opening Night Live at Gamescom to share a few more details about the game, including what players can expect.
"We had this idea for one more story with Geralt for a while, but we couldn't quite figure out how to fit it into our busy schedule," Tost said. "Luckily, our friends from Fool's Theory and they hired a bunch of old veteran Witcher three developers, including my mentor, Peter Jennings, and here we are today."
He continued, saying, "This is Geralt's last adventure before we pass the torch on to Ciri, and we wanted to go out with a bang. So this chain is a weapon that is new in the game, but many people, perhaps hardcore Witcher fans, will realize that this is a weapon we first showed in The Witcher 1 intro, and we will talk about that in many more things here at Gamescom."
On Letten, Tost called it "a whole new, unique region that has a unique identity," filled with quests, new monsters, adventures, and exploration.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
"Just like the things that Witcher fans love," he said. "But it's an almost uncannily idyllic place that, however, has a dark secret lurking just underneath the surface. And as it is a Witcher game, this kind of secret requires a true professional witcher to solve."
Alongside the expansion trailer, the studio also announced The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt Remastered, a free upgrade featuring all-new improvements and revamped gameplay features, arriving on September 29 for all platforms.
The developer also confirmed that all those features will be in Songs of the Past as well.
The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt - Songs of the Past is slated to launch in 2027, followed by The Witcher 4, which CDPR has confirmed is targeting a 2028 release window.

articles.title: ASUS ROG Xbox Ally X20 Launches With $300 Price Premium for OLED and TMR Upgrade
articles.text:
Tuesday, August 25th 2026
	
		
	
	
	
ASUS ROG Xbox Ally X20 Launches With $300 Price Premium for OLED and TMR Upgrade
When ASUS first revealed the ROG Xbox Ally X20 at Computex 2026, it said that the gaming handheld would be available as a bundle with a set of Xreal R1 Edition 20 AR glasses or as a standalone handheld, but pricing and details on the standalone version were still somewhat nebulous, but ASUS has finally announced pricing and imminent pre-order availability for the X20 handheld on both its online store and on Best Buy. 
The standalone handheld gets a price of $1,299.99, which is a $300 price increase over the standard ROG Xbox Ally X. The X20 Anniversary Edition is powered by the same AMD Ryzen AI Z2 Extreme APU, 24 GB of RAM, and 1 TB SSD as the original handheld, but the flashy new smoky translucent chassis isn't the only upgrade. The Xbox Ally X20 features a new 7.4-inch, 120 Hz ROG Nebula HDR OLED display that boasts an increased 1,400 nits of peak brightness and upgraded controller ergonomics.For the ROG Xbox Ally X20 edition, ASUS swapped out the analogue sticks for TMR joysticks, which are generally more sensitive and more reliable, thanks to magnetic sensing instead of potentiometers. The X20 also has redesigned ABXY buttons with more rounded, flush tops that ASUS claims make it easier to move your thumb between the buttons, and the D-pad now has a swappable topper, like an Xbox Elite controller.
