articles.title: Why the global push to break free from Big Tech keeps falling short
articles.text:
In mid-2024, a cybersecurity partner’s mistake led to a global Microsoft Windows outage. It affected 8.5 million Windows devices. Although this represents less than 1% of all Windows machines, it caused major disruptions. Airports were shut down, major airlines experienced widespread delays, and media outlets were unable to broadcast live content. Emergency services in the U.S. were affected, along with banking services, stock markets, petrol stations, retail stores, hospitals and telecommunications companies. The outage starkly illustrated the extent of the world’s dependence on Big Tech.
The question of (digital) sovereignty — and whether democratic governments can still secure it — comes to the fore. Outside the U.S. and China, Big Tech and especially cloud hegemons have significantly eroded digital sovereignty. Technological dependencies extend beyond individuals and private organizations.
In 2024, the U.K. signed a five-year agreement with Microsoft for its digital transformation. The German government has a similar agreement with AWS and its German partner Bechtle AG. AWS is used around the world, from the Australian Bureau of Statistics, to Argentina’s Provincia Bank, the public bank of the Buenos Aires province. In New Zealand, the Department of Internal Affairs holds an all-of-government agreement with Google Cloud. While most of these public sector deals with cloud hegemons go under the radar, a high-profile example was Israel’s $1.2 billion contract with Google and Amazon to develop a private cloud infrastructure. Called Project Nimbus, the initiative came to light after employees from both companies revealed it was designed to support the Israeli military’s use of AI for surveillance and unlawful data collection targeting Palestinians.
These are just a few examples of a global trend in which governments feel compelled to pursue a digital transformation by outsourcing key control technologies to cloud hegemons. Resulting dependencies complicate efforts to regulate them, as governments rely on cloud hegemons for the very technologies that underpin economic governance.
Among the governments implementing industrial policies to counter the dominance of U.S. (and Chinese) Big Tech, three cases stand out: the European Commission and two approaches from emerging economies. None of these initiatives, however, tackles the core issue of intellectual monopolization, and none has, so far, managed to significantly expand digital sovereignty in relation to the cloud giants and other large tech corporations.
The European Commission’s AI Continent Action Plan, released in April 2025, aims to boost AI development in Europe. On the supply side, the EU is investing in “AI factories” comprising public supercomputers, datasets and other services to support the training of AI models and the development of AI applications. The plan also includes AI gigafactories to be established through public-private partnerships. European startups might train their models on EU supercomputers, but they are still likely to deploy them via Big Tech clouds.
By comparison, Brazil and India have both pursued strategies to develop their own digital technology ecosystems. IndiaAI and the Brazilian AI plan place a much stronger emphasis on the role of the public sector in advancing digital sovereignty. Nonetheless, a shared limitation is that they continue to treat the cloud as just infrastructure as a service, and do not fully decouple from Big Tech.
In the case of IndiaAI, a group of advisors to the government that included employees of Intel and Oracle, recommended the creation of alternative AI infrastructure through an initiative dubbed the FutureLab AI Compute Infrastructure. Echoing the European Commission’s AI gigafactories, this would be developed via a public-private partnership. If adopted, the government will proceed in collaboration with Intel and Oracle, thereby perpetuating structural technological dependencies, which include the reliance of its edtech and healthtech services on Oracle infrastructure.
In Brazil, state-owned telecommunications and data companies have pushed for the development of an intermediate layer to provide computing services to the public sector. Beneath this intermediate layer, U.S. Big Tech companies will continue to supply core black-boxed technologies to the Brazilian public sector. As the trajectory of these initiatives illustrates, it seems to be impossible to decouple from cloud hegemons and other U.S. Big Tech. There has been, though, a seemingly successful story.
The Chinese model
China is viewed by many as a model worth emulating precisely because it has built its own digital technologies ecosystem including a cloud market dominated exclusively by Chinese players. But even setting aside concerns about massive surveillance and lack of democracy, the Chinese approach is not fundamentally different from the U.S. Big Tech-dominated system when it comes to intellectual monopolies.
In fact, the Chinese model is based on largely imitating U.S. technologies. Chinese tech giants and AI startups have, so far, preferred to avoid risk, positioning themselves as fast followers that build businesses by capitalizing domestically on U.S. advances in AI. Interviewees from Tencent, NetEase, Pony.ai and Megvii described the strength of Chinese tech firms in similar terms: Chinese tech companies do not go from zero to one, but can scale up previously existing discoveries, going from one to 100 at an incredibly fast speed. They adapt the models of U.S. firms to local conditions in order to “cash up,” as one Tencent software engineer put it. An interviewee from Pony.ai noted that Chinese computer scientists trained abroad, and with experience in Silicon Valley, reinforce this culture of imitation when they return to China or work for Chinese firms from abroad.
Fast imitation has been the most viable strategy for Chinese firms when it comes to AI and the cloud, given their access to a huge protected domestic market, rising geopolitical tensions and the entrenched global structure of corporate power. The experience of HuaweiHuaweiHuawei is a Chinese technology company focused on mobile phones and telecommunications, and is seen as a poster child for China’s global tech ambitions.READ MORE serves as a cautionary tale. Although it forged ahead with 5G, geopolitical backlash curtailed its global market expansion. Washington systematically obstructed Huawei’s efforts to roll out 5G across Western economies, allowing competitors time to replicate the technology and restrict the Chinese telecom giant’s market growth.
Overall, geopolitical tensions restrict the potential for any Chinese technological leapfrogging to translate into global market leadership in AI. In this context, the emergence of DeepSeek, a more affordable model, increases uptake not just among end users, but also especially among developers building AI applications. This benefits U.S. cloud hegemons, as DeepSeek exerts downward pressure on other startups, discouraging them from diversifying or establishing independent ecosystems. It also favours those giants because DeepSeek’s models can be rented as a service on their clouds. DeepSeek does not compete with cloud hegemons or disrupt their core business.
But even if China were to leap ahead of the U.S. in technological terms, this would not represent a victory for the majority. It would simply mark a reshuffling of ruling powers. While the turmoil created by such a reshuffling might momentarily distract political and corporate rulers from tightening their control over the rest of the world, the Chinese model ultimately mirrors that of the U.S. too closely to be celebrated or replicated.
Adapted from “The Rulers: Corporate Power in the Age of AI and the Cloud” by Cecilia Rikap published by Verso Books © 2026 by Cecilia Rikap, and reprinted with permission.

articles.title: The Witcher 3 is getting a remaster
articles.text:
CD Projekt Red is remastering The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, the hit RPG that first launched in 2015, and the updated game will be available starting September 29th. The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered will bring improvements to visuals and combat, a “reimagined” skill tree, and more, and it also includes the first two expansions, Hearts of Stone and Blood and Wine.
The Witcher 3 is getting a remaster
The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered launches in September.
Remastered will be a free upgrade for players who own the base game on GOG, Steam, Epic Games Store, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X / S. With the launch of Remastered, The Witcher 3 will also be coming to the Nintendo Switch 2.
This remastered version of The Witcher 3 (which follows a next-gen upgrade released in 2022) is the start of a big push for the franchise over the next few years. CDPR is set to launch a brand new Witcher 3 expansion, titled Songs of the Past, in 2027, and it’s aiming to release its next mainline Witcher game, The Witcher 4, in 2028.

articles.title: Waymo robotaxis are headed to Munich | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Waymo said Tuesday it plans to launch a robotaxi service in Munich, months after the Alphabet-owned autonomous vehicle company set up an entity in Germany.
The company still must weave its way through mapping and testing, as well as clear regulatory hurdles before it can launch commercial operations.
Waymo will begin, as it has in the other 11 cities where it has commercial robotaxi operations, by first manually driving its vehicles to map the streets of Munich. It will then test its autonomous vehicles with human safety drivers behind the wheel, before removing them. Waymo typically allows its employees, media, and other invited guests to ride in its driverless vehicles at this stage.
The company will eventually open its robotaxis to limited service, and eventually to all riders once it receives the regulatory approval required to operate commercially. Waymo said in a blog post on Tuesday that it is working with Germany’s Federal Motor Transport Authority (KBA), state authorities, and local officials, and expects to open commercial ride-hailing to the public toward the end of 2027.
Waymo’s entry into Germany comes more than five years after the country’s lawmakers adopted legislation to allow driverless vehicles on public roads, and in that process making it the first country in the European Union to create a legal framework for Level 4 autonomous driving. Level 4 autonomy is a designation by the Society of Automobile Engineers (SAE) that means the self-driving system handles all the driving, with no expectation of a human taking over, in certain conditions or environments.
This legal framework has made Germany a hotspot for autonomous vehicle testing. Today, several companies, including Mobileye and Volkswagen, hold permits to test their autonomous vehicles in the country, according to the KBA’s latest data. Waymo does not currently have any permits.
However, the vast majority, including U.K. self-driving startup Wayve, and Israel-based Autobrains, hold Level 3 permits. Level 3, or conditional automated driving, is a system that can handle all the driving within specific operating conditions, such as low speeds on highways, but the driver must be able to take over when needed.
Germany isn’t the only overseas hotspot for AV developers. The U.K., especially London, is shaping up as another robotaxi battleground. Waymo has said it plans to launch a commercial service in London in 2026, which will pit it against Wayve and its partner Uber. Chinese tech giant Baidu has also started testing autonomous vehicles in the city as part of its partnership with Lyft and Freenow.

articles.title: Matthew McConaughey y Woody Harrelson, por fin juntos en el genial tráiler de su nueva serie después de 'True Detective'
articles.text:
Matthew McConaughey y Woody Harrelson, legendarios protagonistas de la primera temporada de True Detective, se reencuentran al fin en una nueva serie. Ambos actores han demostrado siempre una química inigualable y una relación de amistad tremendamente cercana. Por ello, más de diez años después de aquel glorioso éxito de HBO, vuelven a reunirse. Esta vez, en una serie de Apple TV.
Y es que la compañía ha desvelado al fin el tráiler de Brothers, la nueva serie de comedia protagonizada y producida por Matthew McConaughey y Woody Harrelson. En ella, ambos interpretan versiones ficcionalizadas de sí mismos. Su larga amistad se verá amenazada cuando descubren un secreto oculto durante décadas: que quizá sean hermanos. Cuando la boda de la hija de Woody se anula, este reúne a toda la familia y se dirige a Austin para pasar una temporada en el rancho de Matthew.
Pero lo que comenzó como una escapada sanadora se arruina cuando la madre de Matthew, Ma Mac, confiesa accidentalmente el secreto: que los dos amigos podrían ser, en realidad, hermanos. Mientras Woody pone el rancho patas arriba para descubrir la verdad, Matthew se encuentra a sí mismo inmerso en una crisis de identidad muy diferente: la posibilidad de presentarse al cargo de Gobernador de Texas. El resultado es una historia conmovedora, anárquica y divertidísima sobre amistad, familia, fama y la incierta línea que separa el mito de la realidad.
Mira el tráiler de Brothers
Brothers está creada por el showrunner Lee Eisenberg, conocido por su trabajo como guionista y director en The Office, por Cocina con química, por El Jurado o por las películas Bad Teacher y Año Uno. Lo más interesante es que la serie parte de una premisa real. Porque, más allá de la ficción, Matthew McConaughey y Woody Harrelson han reconocido en más de una ocasión de que existe una gran posibilidad de que sean hermanos.
Junto a ellos, el reparto de la serie lo componen Natalie Martinez, Brittany Ishibashi, Nolan Almeida, Ella Grace Helton, Noah Carganilla, Highdee Kuan, Oona Yaffe y Holland Taylor. Brothers se estrenará en Apple TV el 23 de septiembre con el lanzamiento de sus dos primeros capítulos, a los que seguirá uno nuevo cada miércoles hasta el 4 de noviembre.

articles.title: Q&A: The AI costs that could hurt Canadian tech more than a trade war | BetaKit
articles.text:
Canada was thrust into a trade war again this weekend. After the US reportedly tried to change deal terms at the last minute, Canada backed out of a proposed trade agreement. The US then imposed a broad set of tariffs on $28 billion of goods on Saturday, with Canada announcing dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs set to take effect on Sept. 8. It threw businesses into a new wave of uncertainty, and the feds have introduced a $7.5-billion package of new measures to support domestic industries.
Electronics and electrical equipment exports are set to be hit the hardest by tariffs among Canadian industries, according to The Globe and Mail, with Canada exporting roughly $4.4 billion USD ($6.1 billion CAD) worth of products last year. However, there’s a twin cost issue that may hurt the broader industry worse than tariffs. Tech giants pouring billions into AI compute infrastructure have contributed to a shortage in computer memory, driving up random-access memory (RAM) and other hardware prices.
Kevin Jia, the co-founder of Canadian PC maker Quoted Tech Computers, has a front-row seat to both electronics duties and skyrocketing hardware costs. BetaKit spoke to Jia about how Canada’s businesses and consumers should navigate juggling “chipflation” with potential new tariffs.
The following interview has been edited for clarity and length.
How might the collapse of this weekend’s trade talks, and the imposition of fresh tariffs and counter-tariffs, impact AI hardware buyers in Canada?
Any time tariffs come into place, it immediately puts everybody on edge. Everyone gets a little bit more nervous about how the supply chains will work.
But it really comes down to the country of origin for these AI hardware products. While many tech companies are headquartered in the US, like Nvidia and Intel, they don’t manufacture the actual silicon in the device. Sometimes they do some final assembly. Sometimes they don’t.
For example, US Customs and Border Protection treats Quoted Tech’s products as Vietnamese in origin, even though the vast majority of the final product is done in Canada. They will say the identifying factor of a desktop computer is the central processing unit, which is of Vietnamese origin.
Now, why do they do that? I have a suspicion they’re probably trying to play to the tariff code, and that they see Vietnam as kind of a tariff-free zone. That’s purely me speculating.
So how are tariffs really impacting the computing industry?
The tariff code is exceptionally complicated and long, and there are a lot of carve-outs for separate industries. Anybody who has tried to do any major brokerage between the two countries since Donald Trump first imposed new tariffs knows how complicated this is. And getting a definitive answer on anything is like finding a needle in a haystack.
When I saw the 50-percent tariffs and people said the price of computers is going up, I said, “Whoa, in what circumstance?” I also saw that they’re going to tariff Canadian video game consoles. To my knowledge, there are no consoles that are manufactured wholly in Canada. If there is a CPU—and every gaming console has a CPU and a graphics card—those components would be designated as most likely Taiwanese or Vietnamese in origin. When I read that, I was very confused.
The US and Canada base it on a country of origin; who made the original “product” gives it its defining characteristic feature. It doesn’t matter where the final assembly happens; they’re going to find one component that is the designating factor of that product and say, okay, well it happens here.
The new tariffs come alongside computer hardware costs already rising, potentially creating a double impact for consumers. How is the RAM price hike affecting Canadian companies and buyers—both at the hardware level, and then downstream costs of AI in general?
If you’re one of the hyperscalers, the price increases are, truthfully, relatively muted. They are investing billions upon billions of dollars into data center infrastructure. So, for them, a 15- or 20-percent price hike won’t hurt them. They’ve got big contracts that would have been signed way before the price hike.
For the rest of us who are just consuming off the shelf, that’s going to affect everything that you purchase. For a regular Canadian, that means your smartphones, your computers, your tablets—all that’s going to go up. In business, if you’re buying laptops, workstations, servers, all of that is going to be felt at the door. If they’re more RAM- and GPU-heavy, they’re going to feel it worse.
What kind of broad impact does chipflation have on Canada’s startup and tech sector?
The Canadian startup sector is a lot tougher than what they have in the United States and Silicon Valley. There’s just a lot less attention; it’s a lot harder to get funding, and there’s a lot more scrutiny over the projects.
For a lot of these startups that are in AI, that are in deep technology, that are building software, that need access to high-density compute, it’s going to increase their startup costs. Startups are no different than any other business looking to procure hardware. They have a limited budget, and so it’s going to hurt every business trying to get into this space.
How should companies prepare for chipflation and tariff uncertainty? How can they avoid overspending?
The sad reality is that there isn’t a whole lot, truthfully. When it comes down to computer chips, there isn’t a massive market of free-flowing products somewhere else in the world. It’s obviously why Nvidia is the most valuable company in the world.
When customers are shocked by the prices, I say “look, just don’t try to time the market. Buy a computer if you need a computer. You could be waiting until the end of 2027, most likely, before we see a resumption of normality.”
Feature image courtesy Christian Wiediger via Unsplash.

articles.title: Pourquoi le Mac Mini M4 reste une excellente affaire face au nouveau modèle M6
articles.text:
Pourquoi le Mac Mini M4 reste une excellente affaire face au nouveau modèle M6
Probablement la dernière chance d'obtenir le Mini à ce prix
Apple a renouvelé son ordinateur de bureau ultracompact. En sautant la génération M5 pour son modèle d'entrée de gamme, le constructeur intègre directement la puce M6. Cette mise à jour technique s'accompagne toutefois d'une hausse tarifaire marquée, modifiant le positionnement du Mac autrefois le plus abordable du fabricant.
Le nouveau Mac mini M6 s'affiche désormais au tarif de 1049 € dans sa version de base comprenant 16 Go de mémoire vive et 256 Go de stockage. Cette évolution des prix s'explique principalement par le contexte industriel et la hausse des coûts des composants, désignée sous le terme de « rampocalypse ».
À titre de comparaison, la génération précédente équipée de la puce M4 s'était positionnée à 699 € lors de son lancement. Son prix s'était ensuite stabilisé autour de 629 €, connaissant même des baisses ponctuelles à 599 € en octobre 2025.
Des gains de performances et une connectivité révisée
Pour accompagner ce changement de gamme, Apple met en avant les évolutions techniques apportées par le processeur M6. La marque annonce des performances en hausse de 20 % sur la partie processeur (CPU) et de 30 % sur le traitement graphique (GPU) par rapport au modèle M4.
La connectique évolue également avec l'intégration en série d'un port Ethernet 2,5 Gb/s. Le sans-fil passe quant à lui au Wi-Fi 7, bien que la largeur de la bande de fréquence reste limitée à une largeur de 160 MHz sur les appareils de la marque.
Encore quelques M4 disponible
Pour les utilisateurs à la recherche d'un ordinateur compact pour de la bureautique ou des tâches légèrement plus productives, le Mac mini M4 (16 Go / 256 Go) conserve un intérêt financier puisqu'il permet de s'équiper à moindre frais. Ainsi il reste encore quelques pièces chez des revendeurs, notamment chez Amazon à 699 €. Il faut néanmoins composer avec des délais d'approvisionnement rallongés, les disponibilités affichées ne figurant pas avant le mois d'octobre.

articles.title: Kepler Communications’ space-based data centres come online | BetaKit
articles.text:
Following its historic satellite launch earlier this year, Kepler Communications says it has brought online the first commercial space data relay service, effectively creating orbital data centres.
The news: The Toronto-based company announced on Monday that its satellite constellation is now delivering real-time, space-based computing to its commercial and government customers. With this, Kepler said it has brought the first low-Earth orbit satellite system based on an optical relay network online, meaning a Canadian company has beaten out similar projects from big names like Amazon and Starlink.
From the source: “The ‘data centre in the sky’ has moved from fiction to reality!” John Ruffolo, managing partner at Maverix Private Equity and a Kepler investor, wrote in a LinkedIn post.
In his own post, Kepler co-founder and CEO Mina Mitry said the feat felt “surreal.”
“Many have tried to build this before us,” Mitry said. “We’re proud to be the first to make it a commercial reality.”
The context: Each satellite in Kepler’s network is equipped with a minimum of four optical terminals, enabling laser links between space, air, and ground assets. As Mitry described to BetaKit earlier this year, Kepler is essentially pointing a laser at an object the size of a baseball 6,500 kilometres away, and holding it steady while moving at 7.5 kilometres per second.
This relay network allows data to be processed and analyzed directly in space, rather than waiting for a downlink to Earth, effectively turning the satellites into an orbital data centre for space missions. Kepler says this reduces latency, enables the use of AI, and supports autonomous space operations.
Final thought: As demand for compute increases, companies like Google, Starlink, and Amazon are looking to launch orbital data centres to take advantage of solar power and the cold space environment. However, some experts warn the pursuit could pollute the Earth’s atmosphere, while others argue it’s simply impractical. Still, Kepler said it’s set to expand its global optical data relay network in 2028 with a new tranche of spacecraft to support customer demand and data rates up to 100 Gbps.
Feature image courtesy Kepler Communications.

articles.title: AgeLab research inspires an A I startup
articles.text:
AgeLab research inspires an A I startup
Don Yansen ’63
When Don Yansen ’63 arrived at the MIT AgeLab for a study on technology in caregiving for older adults, he didn’t plan to launch another company. But when he heard participants talk about how hard modern devices can be to use, he decided to develop an alternative.
Yansen, a serial entrepreneur who retired to care for his wife, earned an MIT degree in electrical engineering and a master’s in physics from Northeastern. “What I took from MIT was a good education and the feeling I could solve difficult problems,” he says.
One such problem: Many older adults “can’t even use a modern cell phone,” he says, “and very few people can use something like an Apple Watch.” So Kiwi Health, which he founded in October 2024, sells a wristband controlled primarily by voice. Wearers can set reminders, make calls, send texts, and share health data, all without navigating screens. AI helps interpret these commands, accounting for the way voices may change with age. The device also measures health metrics and automatically alerts caregivers to falls.
Yansen’s hope, he says, is that it can “help seniors live the best life that they can.”

articles.title: How GM Canada is Steering a Global Mobility Strategy from Ontario | BetaKit
articles.text:
Anyone who has shared a vehicle knows it involves a little compromise. One driver shifts the seat up, while the other moves the mirrors and drops the steering wheel. It can get frustrating, fast.
For engineers at GM Canada, easing that handoff was a technological challenge worth taking on. Within weeks, the Ontario-based team developed code that uses individual key fobs to identify who has unlocked the vehicle and automatically load that person’s profile, including seat and steering wheel positions, favourite music, and saved destinations. After testing the feature for security, privacy, and other requirements, GM rolled it out across a much larger number of vehicles, wherever they are in the world.
“Canada stands at a very enviable point compared with many parts of the world.”
“We have a communication mechanism across our ecosystem to understand customers’ needs, and our teams are continuously working on identifying, innovating, and rolling out solutions,” said Jack Uppal, GM Canada president and managing director, in an interview with Betakit.
Uppal sees the feature as one small example of a broader transformation underway across the automotive industry. Automakers are becoming more like tech companies, using AI and software to expand what vehicles can do and rethink how they’re designed, driven, and improved over time.
Having led teams in China, India, Singapore, and the Middle East, Uppal has watched technology and mobility evolve at different speeds around the world. From that vantage point, he believes Canada has the talent and research strengths to help lead the next era of software-defined vehicles. That potential is backed by considerable industry investment, with automakers’ in-house R&D spending in Canada reaching $898 million in 2024, quadruple the amount spent a decade earlier.
“Canadian engineering talent is absolutely world-class,” he said, pointing to the country’s technical depth, strong academic foundation, and ability to take ideas beyond the lab and apply them to real-world problems at scale.
“Canada stands at a very enviable point compared with many parts of the world,” he said.
From Ontario to the world
More than 1,100 engineers work across GM Canada’s three Ontario campuses. Teams at the Canadian Technical Centres (CTCs) in Markham and Oshawa develop software and run simulations, while the 55-acre McLaughlin Advanced Technology Track allows them to test systems in real vehicles.
But Uppal is clear that they aren’t building solely for the Canadian market. Depending on the project, engineers here may lead testing or simulation, develop a particular layer of technology, or write code from beginning to end. Those innovations can then be incorporated into vehicles across GM’s wider global operations.
Super Cruise offers an example of how far that work can travel.
The hands-free driving technology—considered to be next-gen cruise control—relies on a combination of real-time cameras, radar, GPS, and precision LiDAR-scanned maps to help equipped vehicles steer, adjust their speed, and change lanes on compatible roads. The process was pioneered by engineers in Markham and has now been used to drive more than 1.6 billion kilometres throughout Canada and the US, according to the company. The same mapping approach is now being adapted for Europe, the Middle East, and South Korea, with the needs of each market considered from the start.
“Before we scale it or even pass it on to a single customer, that product would be built to comply with both the regulatory and customer needs in the markets where we want to sell that feature,” noted Uppal.
The Super Cruise system has also continued to evolve as engineers identify new ways drivers want to use it. Uppal pointed to towing as an example of a need that was particularly visible close to home.
“A lot of people, both in Western Canada and just from a lifestyle perspective, are pulling boats and trailers,” he said.
The original technology didn’t account for a trailer’s additional size, weight, and turning radius. Canadian engineers responded by developing a hands-free towing capability, taking it from “identifying the problem, writing the code, testing the code on the roads, and then being able to deploy it across millions of vehicles in North America.”
While Uppal described trailering as “perhaps more of a North American-relevant question,” he said the solution has been “very well received in many other parts of the world.”
Predictive technology and the future of mobility
Developing new features is one thing. Getting them into millions of vehicles quickly and conveniently is another. Over-the-air updates have changed that, allowing automakers to add or improve features after a vehicle is already on the road. GM reports that more than 4.5 million of its vehicles can currently receive these updates, with that number growing by roughly two million each year.
That can save drivers a trip to the service centre. For Uppal, however, it reflects GM’s broader goal of using software to improve both vehicle performance and the experience behind the wheel.
“Moving billions of people around the world is what we’ve done for the last 100 years. It makes me very confident that we’re going to be a company that’s going to move people for another 100 years.”
“We continue to enhance our advanced driver-assistance systems capability,” he said. “For customers, it’s a driving experience that becomes progressively safer, more intuitive, less stressful.”
Looking ahead, Uppal expects vehicles to move beyond simply responding to information in real time.
“We will be moving from a level of real-time computing and really starting to use AI as our footprint into predictive modelling,” he said.
By recognizing patterns and anticipating driving conditions, these systems could help vehicles perform better in snow, stop faster, and respond more effectively in complex traffic. Uppal also sees the potential to save drivers time and reduce congestion. GM’s near-term plans include deeper use of AI, including Gemini, as well as new technology in the next Chevrolet Silverado and GMC Sierra.
That future won’t be limited to electric vehicles, he added, noting GM will continue investing in both EVs and traditional, internal-combustion vehicles as preferences and technologies evolve.
“We’ll be able to meet the customer and meet their needs where they are, and deliver what they need,” he said.
Through those shifts, Uppal expects Canada—which he described as a “big anchor” in GM’s North American software operations—to remain central to the work. For him, the industry may be changing, but the next era builds on what GM has spent the past century doing.
“Moving billions of people around the world is what we’ve done for the last 100 years,” he said. “It makes me very confident that we’re going to be a company that’s going to move people for another 100 years.”

articles.title: Quand Sophie Adenot dégaine une brosse à dents à quelques euros pour « dépanner » l'ISS à 100 milliards
articles.text:
L’espace est difficile, dit-on. Il est aussi surprenant. On pouvait le noter dans la journée du 25 août 2026, au moment où Sophie Adenot a procédé à sa deuxième sortie extravéhiculaire à l’extérieur de la Station spatiale internationale (ISS). Objectif du jour ? Achever le travail entamé lors d’une précédente EVA survenue le 18 août.
Rappel des faits. Durant cette première sortie dans l’espace, la Française et son collègue américain Anil Menon ont buté sur un obstacle imprévu lors de leur opération de maintenance : des boulons. Résultat, le remplacement d’une vieille antenne de communication n’a pas pu être bouclé à temps. La sortie du 25 août a permis de finir cette installation.
La réparation n’a rien d’anecdotique. Cette antenne, que les ingénieurs de la NASA appellent SGANT (pour Space-to-Ground Antenna), fait transiter les communications et les données entre l’ISS et le centre de contrôle de Houston, au Texas. Depuis novembre 2025, l’une des deux antennes de ce type ne fonctionnait plus.
La Station n’était pas coupée du monde pour autant, mais elle avait perdu une redondance précieuse, ce filet de sécurité qui permet de continuer à communiquer si un équipement lâche. Le 18 août, Sophie Adenot et son coéquipier de la NASA avaient donc réussi à retirer l’antenne défaillante avant de faire face à ces vieux boulons tenaces.
Cette fois, tout est bien qui finit bien. Après deux EVA qui ont chacune duré environ six heures et demie, l’installation en deux temps de l’antenne a pu être achevée. La Française et l’Américain ont pu ensuite rentrer en toute sécurité, et toute l’opération est un succès : l’Agence spatiale européenne a confirmé le bon fonctionnement de la nouvelle antenne.
La brosse à dents, un classique de la débrouille orbitale
C’est justement pendant cette sortie, que l’on pouvait suivre en direct via un flux vidéo ou grâce aux mises à jour régulières des agences spatiales, que Sophie Adenot a dégainé cette fameuse brosse à dents. C’est ce que racontait l’ESA dans l’une des actualités partagées sur X (ex-Twitter). « L’outil inattendu du jour », a-t-elle d’ailleurs glissé.
Cet ustensile, dont l’usage est pourtant parfaitement décrit par son nom même, n’a évidemment pas servi à nettoyer les quenottes d’un astronaute. Il s’agissait ici d’appliquer un peu de graisse sur des inserts de boulons, juste à côté de l’emplacement de l’antenne, afin de faciliter les manœuvres de vissage et de dévissage.
On peine à croire qu’un ustensile aussi basique ait été utilisé au cours d’une intervention que l’on imagine forcément de pointe, et très technique, compte tenu du contexte : un laboratoire orbital, pressurisé, exposé au vide spatial, à 400 km d’altitude et filant autour de la Terre à près de 28 000 km/h. Bien sûr, on n’imagine que des outils de bricolage très high-tech.
Mais ce serait oublier l’esprit de débrouille et de bricolage qui habite les astronautes et les agences spatiales, et plus particulièrement la NASA. Surtout, ce type de système D n’a rien d’une première. En 2012 déjà, l’Américaine Sunita Williams et le Japonais Akihiko Hoshide avaient sauvé une réparation électrique de l’ISS avec une brosse à dents.
Elle avait été fixée au bout d’une tige pour, là encore, nettoyer et lubrifier un boulon coincé. Même histoire, ou presque : un boulon têtu, une deuxième sortie imprévue ajoutée au planning, et un objet à quelques euros qui dépanne une station qui a coûté plus de cent milliards de dollars (environ 85 milliards d’euros).
Ce genre de couac fait partie du métier, mais cela impose une très (très) grande précaution d’usage. On ne manipule pas une brosse à dents dans l’espace comme on la manipule sur Terre. Lâché par mégarde dans le vide, l’ustensile risquerait de devenir un projectile mortel pour les satellites ou même pour l’ISS et ses occupants, en orbitant à toute allure autour de la Terre.
C’est aussi pour cela qu’elle était reliée à un cordon.

articles.title: Building the logistics backbone for India's next growth phase
articles.text:
Hexalog
View Brand Publisher
Building the logistics backbone for India's next growth phase
As manufacturing expands and global supply chains evolve, India's logistics ecosystem is becoming a strategic advantage. Infrastructure, technology, and integrated platforms are helping businesses move goods faster, smarter, and more efficiently.
For years, logistics was viewed as a support function, moving goods from one point to another. Today, it has become a strategic business priority. When trade routes are disrupted, tariffs shift, or manufacturing hubs face uncertainty, resilient logistics networks keep businesses running. They influence everything from customer experience and delivery timelines to where companies manufacture and how they participate in global trade.
The shift comes at a pivotal time for India.
As manufacturers diversify production beyond traditional hubs, India is emerging as a key player in the next phase of global supply chains.
But attracting factories is only part of the opportunity. Equally important is building a logistics ecosystem that can connect manufacturing hubs with domestic and international markets through modern infrastructure, digital coordination, and integrated supply networks.
The question is no longer whether India will play a larger role in global supply chains, but how central that role can become.
From manufacturing destination to supply chain hub
Several global and domestic trends are driving this shift. Geopolitical tensions, changing trade alliances, and a renewed focus on supply chain resilience are prompting businesses to reduce their dependence on concentrated manufacturing hubs.
At the same time, the China+1 strategy is evolving. Instead of adding a single manufacturing base outside China, many companies are now expanding across multiple countries to spread risk further.
India is already seeing the impact.
Global manufacturers are expanding operations across sectors such as electronics, engineering goods, and pharmaceuticals. Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes continue to boost manufacturing, while electronics exports are growing steadily. Trade agreements with major markets, including the European Union and the United States, are expected to create new freight corridors, expand cross-border trade, and further integrate India into global supply chains.
Manufacturing growth, however, also places greater demands on logistics. Every new factory, export order, and shipment depends on a network capable of moving goods efficiently across the country and beyond.
Building the backbone
India's logistics transformation has been underway for several years, with sustained investment in roads, railways, ports, freight corridors, and multimodal infrastructure steadily improving connectivity.
Government initiatives such as PM Gati Shakti and the National Logistics Policy are enabling more integrated planning while supporting seamless movement across road, rail, ports, and inland waterways. Together, these initiatives are helping reduce logistics costs, improve connectivity, and make Indian manufacturing more competitive.
The country's warehousing network is also expanding. Modern warehouses, automation-ready distribution centers, and cold-chain facilities are making it easier to support ecommerce, exports, and high-value manufacturing.
Physical infrastructure, however, is only part of the equation.
As supply chains become more complex, businesses also need logistics providers that can connect freight forwarding, customs, warehousing, fulfillment, and transportation into a single, coordinated system.
Companies such as Hexalog are helping address that need by providing these services together under one contract, giving businesses a more connected way to manage India's growing logistics ecosystem.
The opportunity lies in orchestration
As India's logistics network expands, the next challenge is no longer simply moving more goods. It is coordinating increasingly complex supply chains efficiently.
Warehousing illustrates how the sector is changing. What was once primarily a storage function has evolved into a value-added service. Manufacturers increasingly expect logistics partners to handle quality checks, packaging, kitting, assembly, inventory management, and fulfillment closer to production hubs and end customers. Instead of working with multiple vendors across the supply chain, businesses are looking for integrated partners that can bring these services together.
Multimodal logistics presents another opportunity.
As dedicated freight corridors, Bharatmala highways, Sagarmala ports, and multimodal logistics parks become more closely connected, companies have greater flexibility in how they move freight. Rail can be used for long-distance transport, with road networks handling last-mile delivery, helping reduce costs while improving speed and reliability.
Companies such as Hexalog use AI to recommend transport modes and routes based on cost, transit time, and potential disruptions, enabling businesses to optimize shipments without adding operational complexity.
Cross-border logistics is evolving as well.
As exports continue to grow, customs clearance is becoming a competitive advantage rather than simply a compliance requirement. Faster documentation, digital workflows, and closer coordination can significantly reduce delays, particularly for sectors such as electronics, engineering goods, pharmaceuticals, and textiles, where speed is critical.
Hexalog integrates customs into the broader logistics journey, from documentation and compliance to freight movement, helping businesses make cross-border shipments faster, more predictable, and easier to manage.
Visibility and resilience become competitive advantages
As supply chains grow more complex, businesses want one view of them, not five providers to coordinate across freight forwarding, customs, warehousing, fulfilment, last-mile delivery, and reverse logistics. “A supply chain that only works when nothing goes wrong isn't a supply chain. It's a bet,” says Dibyanshu Tripathi, CEO & Co-founder, Hexalog.
Companies such as Hexalog combine these capabilities within a single AI-powered ecosystem, giving businesses one view of shipments, inventory, documentation, and logistics operations instead of requiring them to manage multiple systems.
Resilience has become just as important.
Recent disruptions—from shipping delays in the Red Sea to changing trade regulations and geopolitical uncertainty—have demonstrated that supply chains must be designed to adapt as conditions change.
AI is playing an increasingly important role in that shift. By combining real-time visibility with intelligent route planning and proactive disruption, management problems get flagged early, alternatives get surfaced fast, and shipments keep moving even when the plan changes mid-transit.
For businesses, the result is a supply chain that is not only more efficient but also better equipped to respond when unexpected challenges arise.
Technology powering the next phase of logistics
Technology is becoming central to modern logistics.
Artificial intelligence, predictive analytics, and digital orchestration are helping logistics providers optimize routes, automate documentation, improve inventory planning, and make faster operational decisions across increasingly complex supply chains.
As a result, businesses are looking for logistics partners that do more than move freight. They want partners that can help orchestrate their supply chains end to end.
Hexalog is built around that approach. It brings together freight forwarding, customs clearance, warehousing, fulfillment, value-added centers, last-mile delivery, reverse logistics, and AI-driven optimization within a single connected ecosystem.
Instead of managing fragmented logistics processes across multiple providers, businesses gain a unified view of their operations, helping them improve visibility, move faster, and make better-informed decisions.
India’s logistics opportunity extends well beyond moving larger volumes of goods. As manufacturing expands and global supply chains evolve, the focus is shifting toward building an ecosystem that is connected, resilient, and ready for the demands of international trade.
The foundations are already in place. Investments in infrastructure are improving connectivity, manufacturing capacity continues to grow, and new trade agreements are opening up fresh opportunities for exports and cross-border commerce.
The next phase will depend on how efficiently businesses can move goods across these networks. Companies that bring together infrastructure, technology, and supply chain services will play an increasingly important role in helping businesses navigate this growing complexity while strengthening India's position in global trade.

articles.title: On a trouvé l'ultrabook parfait pour la rentrée (et il profite d'une baisse de prix historique)
La Fenix 9 monte en puissance, la Fenix 9 Pro en résistance : Garmin sort le grand jeu pour amateurs de sports outdoor
articles.text:
La Fenix 9 monte en puissance, la Fenix 9 Pro en résistance : Garmin sort le grand jeu pour amateurs de sports outdoor
Deux ans après le lancement de la Fenix 8, Garmin renouvelle sa gamme de montres connectées outdoor avec la sortie simultanée des Fenix 9 et Fenix 9 Pro. Au menu : des boîtiers renforcés, des écrans plus lumineux, de nouvelles fonctionnalités et des performances accrues. Voici les nouveautés de ces deux smartwatches haut de gamme commercialisées à partir de 999 €.
Il fallait s’en douter. Car il y a deux ans presque jour pour jour - le 27 août 2024 - Garmin officialisait son excellente montre outdoor polyvalente, la Fenix 8. Un modèle haut de gamme pensé pour des utilisateurs exigeants, qui a d’ailleurs eu droit un an plus tard à une déclinaison Pro intégrant un écran Micro-Led, le support de la connectivité satellite et la prise en charge d’une eSIM. C’est aujourd’hui l’heure du renouvellement de la gamme, puisque le fabricant américain présente la Fenix 9, mais aussi la Fenix 9 Pro simultanément.
Pour le cas de la Fenix 9 Pro, du nouveau est à chercher du côté du design. Exit les éléments en plastique : le boîtier de la nouvelle montre est entièrement conçu en titane, pour mieux assurer sa résistance aux chocs. La montre intègre un écran reposant sur la technologie Amoled. ll faut rappeler que la Fenix 8 Pro était proposée en Micro-Led (4500 cd/m² annoncés) ou Amoled (2000 cd/m² maximum) : la nouvelle venue promet jusqu’à 3000 cd/m². Une bonne nouvelle, dans la mesure où les modèles concurrents - Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 et Apple Watch Ultra 3 - dépassent de leur côté les 3000 cd/m². Toujours au rayon de l’affichage, Garmin n’y va pas de main morte : l’écran de la Fenix 9 Pro 51 mm atteint 1,5 pouce, quand la Fenix 8 Pro, pourtant loin d’être un petit modèle, pointait à 1,4 pouce. Un agrandissement obtenu ”sans agrandir la taille du boîtier”, indique Garmin. On note également l’intégration d’une nouvelle Led dédiée à l’éclairage nocturne, qui ajoute le vert aux blanc et rouge déjà disponibles.
Côté fonctions, on retrouve le support du LTE, qui permet d’envoi de notification LiveTrack au lancement d’activités choisies, mais aussi le partage de la localisation pendant les activités. La connectivité satellite s’ajoute au LTE et permet d’ailleurs d’obtenir des bulletins météo précisément localisés, utiles notamment à la pratique de sports outdoor, type trail. La connectivité satellite, qui p asse par le service InReach de Garmin, s’ouvre de surcroît à tous les formats de la montre : ses versions 43, 47 et 51 mm en sont dotées (en option), alors qu’elle était réservée au modèle de 51 mm. En revanche, il n’est plus cette année question de mouture à écran micro-LED.
Garmin Fenix 9 Pro
Une Fenix 9 plus puissante et mieux protégée contre les chocs
La Fenix 9 classique présente, elle aussi, son lot de nouveautés. Elle aussi proposée en formats 43, 47 et 51 mm, la tocante profite d’une luminosité de 2000 cd/m², mais surtout d’un afficheur protégé par une vitre saphir, tandis que la Fenix 8 alternait entre Gorilla Glass 3 et saphir selon les versions. Son boîtier, qui n’est certes pas en titane, gagne une étanchéité jusqu’à 40 mètres dans le cadre de plongée. Il inclut désormais 64 Go de stockage, soit le double de la Fenix 8, pour stocker des cartographies bien sûr, mais aussi de la musique à écouter hors-connexion. Dans l’ensemble, Garmin annonce un gain en fluidité général, et une rapidité accrue à l’affichage de cartographies, notamment grâce à une RAM augmentée de 50 %. Précisons que comme la Fenix 9 Pro, la Fenix 9 est annoncée avec 10 jours d’autonomie, soit peu ou prou le lot habituel des montres Garmin.
Les différentes fonctionnalités inédites de la Fenix 9 sont partagées avec celles du modèle Pro. On retrouve le suivi des Stamina qui, dans le langage de Garmin, correspond à un indice de forme mis à jour en temps réel en cours d’entraînement ; mais aussi la mesure de davantage de données pendant des sessions de rameur (dont la VO2 Max).
Les prix enfin. Les Fenix n’ont rien de modèles d’entrée de gamme, et se monnaient à partir de 999 € pour la Fenix 9 43 ou 47 mm (1099 € en 51 mm). Le modèle Pro, lui, coûte un minimum de 1099 € sans inReach, auxquels il faut ajouter 100 € pour une connectivité satellite. Au plus cher, la tocante coûte 1399 €, en 51 mm avec inReach.

articles.title: Brussels-based MAASH secures €12.15 million to take mycoprotein production to industrial scale | EU-Startups
articles.text:
MAASH, a Brussels-based fermentation company specialising in the development and production of mycoproteins for the food industry, has secured a €12.15 million funding package combining equity investment and public financing.
The package includes a €5.85 million equity raise from five new investors: Ambra Capital, InvestPro, Bpifrance, Amorçage Industriel, Nordzucker and Tereos. It also includes €4.3 million in support from Bpifrance through the Première Usine programme and a €2 million Bpifrance loan through its Prêt d’Amorçage Investissement, supported by France 2030.
Frédéric Van Gansberghe, co-founder and Chairman of the board, said, “Our industrial fermentation experience, combined with the arrival of our new partners, will allow us to move quickly through our technical and commercial scale-up.”
Founded in 2021 by Frédéric Van Gansberghe and Gaspard Gilbert, MAASH is a BioTech startup focused on developing mycoprotein as a sustainable ingredient for the food industry.
According to the company, it precisely controls fermentation parameters such as temperature, pH, and oxygen supply to ensure optimal yield while preserving the mycoprotein’s functional and sensory qualities. It collaborates with companies to “enhance” its products by incorporating its mycoprotein, reducing meat content by 10 to 30%, or developing vegan and vegetarian options.
The company states that with LoCylia™, its fermentation-derived mycoprotein, it is positioning itself as a B2B ingredient supplier for the food industry.
MAASH also revealed that it is moving from project development to execution, two years after acquiring the former Metabolic Explorer site in Carling-Saint-Avold.
The Belgian startup has also appointed Samah Garringer as its CEO, who will join the company in September 2026. She has more than 25 years of international experience spanning food, ingredients, nutrition and industrial scale-up, and has held executive roles at DSM, Avril Group and ENOUGH Foods.
Samah Garringer, incoming CEO, said, “I am thrilled to join MAASH at this pivotal moment. Together with the team and our new partners, we will deliver the pre-industrial project, accelerate commercial rollout and build a resilient, cost-competitive platform to bring nutritious, sustainable mycoprotein to market at scale.”
As part of this transition, Gaspard Gilbert, MAASH’s current Managing Director and co-founder, will take on the role of Chief Commercial Officer, leading the company’s commercial relationships and strategic partnerships, while also serving as acting Chief Finance Officer.
Gilbert said, “Acquiring the former Metex site gave us an industrial base. Over the past two years, we have worked to turn that base into a credible and executable project. This financing marks an important step in that journey: we now have the partners, resources and leadership in place to move from preparation to industrial deployment. The appointment of Samah Garringer as CEO reflects the same ambition – giving MAASH the industrial, human and commercial capabilities it needs to scale.”
The funding will support the launch of MAASH’s 12 m³ demonstration plant in Carling-Saint-Avold, France, and prepare the company for further scale-up to 10,000 tons of annual industrial production.

articles.title: SpaceX baut Weltraumbahnhof für 100 Milliarden Dollar
articles.text:
Tausende Starts pro Jahr: SpaceX plant neuen Weltraumbahnhof für 100 Milliarden Dollar
Sieben Jahre lang hat SpaceX eigenen Angaben zufolge nach einem geeigneten Areal für seinen geplanten neuen Weltraumbahnhof gesucht. Einen Standort, der ausreichend Platz für die geplanten Startrampen und den benötigten Treibstoff bietet, hat Elon Musks Raumfahrtfirma jetzt im US-Bundesstaat Louisiana gefunden.
Weltraumbahnhof an der Golfküste
Wie die für die Ansiedlung neuer Unternehmen zuständige Behörde Louisiana Economic Development gemeinsam mit SpaceX mitteilte, soll der Weltraumbahnhof im County Vermilion Parish am Golf von Mexiko errichtet werden. Dort sollen künftig tausende Raketenstarts pro Jahr möglich sein.
SpaceX hat angekündigt, bis zu 100 Milliarden Dollar in die Hand nehmen zu wollen. Tausende Jobs sollen in den kommenden Jahren in der wenig entwickelten Region geschaffen werden – inklusive hoher Gehälter, die weit über dem vor Ort üblichen Niveau liegen.
SpaceX will neue Anlage ab 2027 bauen
Mit den Bauarbeiten will der Konzern 2027 beginnen. Für 2029 sind die ersten Raketenstarts vorgesehen. „Wir bereiten den Bau eines Weltraumbahnhofs vor, der bisher nur in der Science-Fiction existierte“, so SpaceX-Gründer und CEO Musk. Den Startplatz nannte er „einen der inspirierendsten Orte unseres Planeten“.
Zuvor hatte sich SpaceX bereiterklärt, in Zusammenarbeit mit dem Bundesstaat eine Küstenrenaturierung zu realisieren. Dabei soll das Marschland wiederhergestellt und sichergestellt werden, das die Feuchtgebiete rund um die neue Anlage vor Stürmen geschützt sind, wie CNBC schreibt.
Kritik an Umweltverstößen in Texas
An seinem ersten Standort, der Starbase-Gemeinde mit Weltraumbahnhof, Raketenfabrik und dem Dorf Boca Chica in Texas, war SpaceX aufgrund von Umweltverstößen mit Klagen und Geldstrafen konfrontiert worden. Zudem gab es teils heftige Kritik aus der Bevölkerung.
Beim ersten Testflug seiner Starship-Rakete war die Startrampe explodiert und das Raumschiff in der Luft verglüht. Betonbrocken waren in ein nahegelegenes Nist- und Wandergebiet gestürzt. Außerdem hatten die Explosionen einen Waldbrand ausgelöst. Zudem soll SpaceX auf seiner Startanlage in Texas wiederholt gegen den Clean Water Act des Bundesstaats verstoßen haben.

articles.title: Testamos! Confira o review completo do Galaxy Watch 9
articles.text:
A Samsung lançou recentemente a nova linha de relógios inteligentes e o Olhar Digital teve a oportunidade de testar o Galaxy Watch 9. O smartwatch tem sensores avançados para monitoramento de dados de saúde e atividades físicas e conta com recursos que permitem até deixar o celular em casa na hora de treinar.
Confira abaixo nossa análise completa e saiba para que tipo de usuário ele vale a pena:
Samsung Galaxy Watch 9: principais características
- Tamanhos: 40 mm e 44 mm
- Tela: Super AMOLED de 3.000 nits com cristal de safira
- Processador: Snapdragon Wear Elite
- Memória e Armazenamento: 2 GB de RAM e 32 GB internos
- Bateria: 300 mAh (40 mm) e 425 mAh (44 mm)
- Conectividade: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth 5.3, NFC e LTE (eSIM opcional)
- Sensores: Frequência cardíaca, ECG, bioimpedância, SpO2 e temperatura
- GPS: Dupla frequência (L1 + L5)
- Resistência: 5 ATM (50 metros), IP68 e certificação militar
Como é o Samsung Galaxy Watch 9
O Galaxy Watch 9 mantém o design conhecido de modelos anteriores da linha, com o formato redondo e as bordas levemente curvadas para encaixar bem no pulso. Essa curva também ajuda os sensores traseiros a ficarem bem encostados na pele, melhorando a leitura das informações ao longo do dia.
As pulseiras são removíveis e podem ser substituídas de acordo com a vontade do usuário. Como é leve (pesa menos de 35 gramas), fica confortável no braço durante o dia todo e não incomoda na hora de dormir.
O display usa um painel Super AMOLED com brilho máximo de 3.000 nits, sendo perfeitamente legível mesmo debaixo do sol forte. Em relação ao Watch 8 do ano passado, as bordas ao redor do visor ficaram mais finas, aproveitando o melhor o espaço da parte frontal da tela. Dois botões laterais auxiliam a navegação pelo aparelho, que também pode ser feita pela touchscreen.
A proteção oferecida pelo vidro de cristal de safira evita arranhões acidentais e aumenta a durabilidade do relógio, que também vem com proteção contra água e poeira, podendo inclusive ser submerso em água a até 50 metros (5 ATM).
Usando o Galaxy Watch 9
Por dentro, a Samsung equipou o Galaxy Watch 9 com o processador Snapdragon Wear Elite, que oferece desempenho de ponta e roda o sistema operacional com velocidade e sem engasgos, seja ao abrir aplicativos ou ao alternar entre as telas. O armazenamento interno é de 32 GB para guardar músicas, aplicativos e mais.
O Galaxy Watch 9 faz tudo aquilo que se espera de um smartwatch desta categoria: ele pode disparar a câmera do smartphone a distância, recebe notificações do celular, permite atender chamadas telefônicas direto no pulso e mais. O acesso à loja de apps Play Store pode ser feito diretamente pelo smartwatch, permitindo baixar e instalar novos apps a qualquer momento sem depender do celular.
Ele também responde a comandos de voz e vem até com um novo recurso voltado para a IA Gemini do Google: basta levantar o pulso e falar algo para o assistente virtual entrar em ação. É um recurso conveniente para quem não quer precisar tirar o celular do bolso e abrir o aplicativo quando quer fazer uma busca rápida.
A bateria segue como um dos pontos fracos do aparelho: ela dificilmente dura muito mais do que um dia, e é bastante provável que você precise carregar sempre pela manhã. O carregamento é feito por indução pela base magnética que acompanha o produto na caixa e não é exatamente dos mais rápidos.
Monitoramento de saúde e atividades físicas
Quem compra um smartwatch não está em busca simplesmente de um aparelho para ver a horas, e quer sempre algo a mais. O Galaxy Watch 9 segue os passos de tantos modelos do mercado e vem com diversos sensores para monitoramento de atividades físicas e índices de saúde.
Os sensores na parte de baixo do relógio monitoram batimentos cardíacos, nível de oxigênio no sangue, estresse, composição corporal e eletrocardiograma. Na hora de dormir, ele monitora fases do seu sono, identifica se você roncou (nesse caso, é preciso deixar o celular por perto) e busca sinais de apneia.
O sistema do Galaxy Watch 9 pega todos esses dados e transforma em notas simples para você entender como está a saúde física. E, claro, é sempre importante lembrar que um smartwatch não substitui um médico de verdade e esses índices devem ser usados mais como referência do que para diagnóstico. Afinal, pode acontecer dele sofrer com algumas falhas no registro automático.
As informações coletadas pelo smartwatch podem ser visualizadas pelo aplicativo Samsung Health. Aqui segue um problema que já estava presente em outros relógios da marca, que restringe algumas funções a smartphones da linha Galaxy. Caso você não esteja no ecossistema da Samsung, é provável que o Galaxy Watch 9 não possa ser plenamente aproveitado.
Para atividades físicas, o relógio reconhece automaticamente caminhadas, corridas e treinos de academia, e começa a registrar informações sem que você precise fazer nada. Ao terminar a atividade, ele mostra sua frequência cardíaca, o tempo de treino e uma estimativa de quantas calorias você queimou.
Como vem com GPS integrado, o Galaxy Watch 9 consegue gravar todo o percurso da sua caminhada ou corrida ao ar livre sem que você precisa levar o celular junto — e o GPS de dupla frequência consegue rastrear muito bem a sua rota, mesmo em áreas com prédios muito altos ou em trilhas, algo que outros smartwatches podem deixar a desejar. Como também é resistente a imersões na água, pode ser usada durante a natação sem que isso prejudique o funcionamento do aparelho.
O relógio também avalia o cansaço do seu corpo com base nas últimas atividades. Ele usa esses dados para avisar quando é hora de descansar ou quando você tem energia para pegar mais pesado nos treinos.
Para quem o Galaxy Watch 9 é indicado?
Tendo como ponto forte um desempenho de ponta, uma tela de alta qualidade e sensores precisos, incluindo um GPS de banda dupla, o Galaxy Watch 9 é uma excelente opção para quem busca um smartwatch para acompanhar índices de saúde e monitorar atividades físicas. Ele é leve, encaixa bem no pulso, pode ser usado mesmo longe do celular e tem excelente integração com o ecossistema da Samsung.
Porém, as restrições em dispositivos que não seja da própria Samsung acaba limitando um pouco as possibilidades de uso para quem está fora do ecossistema da marca. A bateria segue como um dos pontos fracos, e dificilmente você passará mais de um dia sem precisar recarregar o aparelho. Isso também deve ser levado em consideração, já que quem passa longos períodos de tempo fazendo caminhadas, por exemplo, corre o risco de ficar sem bateria no meio do caminho.
